options.B: Securing health resources and equitable care for patients
options.C: Diagnosing rare tropical medical conditions
options.D: Managing hospital financial budgets and records

explanation: Health advocacy focuses on acting for patients to ensure they receive necessary resources and fair treatment. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h1)

question: Why is advocacy particularly vital in primary health care settings?

options.A: It eliminates all administrative hospital delays completely
options.B: It addresses systemic gaps affecting vulnerable populations
options.C: it generates direct revenue for local health clinics
options.D: It replaces the need for direct bedside nursing care

explanation: Primary care nurses often encounter systemic shortages and must advocate to protect vulnerable groups from falling through gaps. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h1)

question: The principle of empowering patients in advocacy means what?

options.A: Taking over all health decisions on behalf of the family
options.B: Enabling communities to articulate their own health needs
options.C: Forcing patients to comply with hospital admission policies
options.D: Handling legal court cases for injured community members

explanation: Empowerment equips people to voice their concerns rather than relying solely on others to speak for them. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h2)

question: Holding health systems responsible for public health outcomes demonstrates which advocacy principle?

options.A: Confidentiality
options.B: Paternalism
options.C: Accountability
options.D: Beneficence

explanation: Accountability ensures that authorities and institutions answer for the health services they provide or fail to provide. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h2)

question: What is the first step required for an impactful health advocacy initiative?

options.A: Accurate identification of community health needs
options.B: Distribution of financial grants to local politicians
options.C: Construction of large tertiary referral hospitals
options.D: Immediate legal prosecution of corrupt health officials

explanation: Advocacy must be grounded in real data and verified community problems rather than mere assumptions. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h3)

question: A community nurse notices a sudden rise in childhood diarrhea. What action should occur first?

options.A: Protest outside the state governor's office immediately
options.B: Order expensive laboratory equipment from abroad
options.C: Close down all local food markets in the neighborhood
options.D: Gather data through community surveys to find the root cause

explanation: Before launching advocacy, the nurse must investigate and collect data to understand the exact nature of the health gap. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h3)

question: Tailoring communication messages in health advocacy depends primarily on what factor?

options.A: The specific audience being addressed
options.B: The international laws governing trade
options.C: The font size used in written reports
options.D: The personal mood of the nurse advocate

explanation: Different groups, from local villagers to high-ranking officials, require customized language and approaches. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h4)

question: Successful negotiation during advocacy meetings typically relies on achieving what outcome?

options.A: Finding common ground where community and policy goals align
options.B: Demanding total capitulation without compromise from leaders
options.C: Threatening legal action for every minor administrative delay
options.D: Ignoring opposing viewpoints to push personal agendas faster

explanation: Effective negotiation builds consensus by showing how supporting health initiatives benefits both the public and decision-makers. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h4)

question: Why is coalition building necessary in large-scale health advocacy?

options.A: It removes the need for community health assessments
options.B: It transfers all financial liabilities to the government
options.C: It guarantees automatic promotion for participating nurses
options.D: It pools resources and amplifies the collective voice

explanation: Working together with diverse groups strengthens the advocacy campaign through shared strength and resources. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h5)

question: A nurse wants to improve routine immunization uptake in a rural area. Which group should be engaged first?

options.A: International pharmaceutical manufacturing corporations
options.B: Private corporate banking executives
options.C: Federal airline pilots and aviation workers
options.D: Local traditional and religious leaders

explanation: Traditional and religious leaders wield strong influence over community members and greatly affect acceptance of health programs. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h5)

question: What marks the starting point of designing a structured advocacy campaign?

options.A: Setting clear objectives and identifying decision-makers
options.B: Purchasing expensive television broadcast stations
options.C: Filing formal complaints with international courts
options.D: Printing customized uniforms for all participating nurses

explanation: A campaign must begin with clear goals and a precise target audience to direct its activities effectively. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h6)

question: Why is maintaining message consistency important throughout an advocacy campaign?

options.A: It ensures compliance with international maritime laws
options.B: It prevents confusion among the public and authorities
options.C: It reduces the total financial cost of printing flyers
options.D: It eliminates the need for any community feedback

explanation: Clear and consistent messaging ensures that the core demand of the campaign is easily understood and remembered. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common hurdle faced by health advocates?

options.A: Entrenched bureaucratic delays within health ministries
options.B: Apathy and resistance from local community members
options.C: Fear of professional victimization or intimidation
options.D: Instant approval and generous funding from authorities

explanation: Instant approval is rare in advocacy; advocates typically struggle against bureaucracy, apathy, and resistance. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h7)

question: How do professional nursing bodies help individual nurses facing advocacy resistance?

options.A: They offer immunity from all civil and criminal laws
options.B: They provide direct international political appointments
options.C: They take over all clinical shift duties indefinitely
options.D: They provide a protective alliance and collective backing

explanation: Professional associations offer safety in numbers and institutional support when nurses face resistance or intimidation. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h7)

question: What is evaluated when assessing the long-term outcome of a health advocacy initiative?

options.A: How many hours the project coordinator spent resting
options.B: The exact brand of megaphones used during rallies
options.C: The total number of colored posters printed last week
options.D: Lasting changes like improved health indices or new policies

explanation: Long-term outcomes measure sustainable impact, such as policy shifts or measurable improvements in community health. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h8)

question: Why is it necessary to evaluate advocacy initiatives despite long timeframes for results?

options.A: To satisfy strict international tax auditing standards
options.B: To punish team members who failed to meet targets
options.C: To secure immediate promotion to hospital management
options.D: To refine future strategies and demonstrate accountability

explanation: Evaluation helps advocates learn what worked, improve future approaches, and prove that resources were used responsibly. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T7#GNS124_U4_T7_h8)

question: What is the primary goal of health advocacy in primary health care?

options.A: Influencing policy and resource allocation
options.B: Managing hospital financial budgets
options.C: Writing medical research journals
options.D: Treating acute tropical infections

explanation: Advocacy aims to drive systemic changes in policy and resource distribution to benefit community health rather than just delivering direct clinical treatment. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T8#GNS124_U4_T8_h1)

question: How does health advocacy differ from standard health education?

options.A: Advocacy changes systemic conditions while education focuses on individual knowledge
options.B: Education requires policy changes while advocacy requires clinical prescriptions
options.C: Advocacy only uses mass media while education uses face-to-face talks
options.D: Education targets government officials while advocacy targets individual patients

explanation: Health education teaches individuals about healthy habits, whereas advocacy tackles the broader environmental and policy barriers affecting health. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T8#GNS124_U4_T8_h1)

question: Who represents the primary audience in a health advocacy campaign?

options.A: Patients admitted to the surgical ward
options.B: Junior community health extension workers
options.C: Students in nursing training institutions
options.D: Decision-makers with power to create change

explanation: The primary audience consists of the specific people who hold the authority to approve policies or release funds. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T8#GNS124_U4_T8_h2)

question: A nurse wants local government funds for a primary health center. Who is the primary audience?

options.A: Ward health committee youth leaders
options.B: The Local Government Chairman
options.C: Local primary school pupils
options.D: Market women associations

explanation: The local government chairman holds direct authority over local council funds, making them the primary decision-making target for budget allocation. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T8#GNS124_U4_T8_h2)

question: What are the three essential elements of a compelling advocacy message?

options.A: Problem, solution, and benefit
options.B: Diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis
options.C: Past, present, and future
options.D: Introduction, body, and conclusion

explanation: An effective message clearly defines what the problem is, what action is needed to fix it, and the positive outcome of taking that action. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T8#GNS124_U4_T8_h3)

question: Why should nurses avoid heavy medical jargon when addressing community stakeholders?

options.A: It violates professional hospital documentation standards
options.B: It increases the financial cost of printing flyers
options.C: It proves that the nurse lacks proper clinical training
options.D: It obscures the human impact and reduces message clarity

explanation: Jargon alienates non-medical stakeholders and distracts from the core community need being presented. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T8#GNS124_U4_T8_h3)

question: What makes a Call to Action strong and effective in health advocacy?

options.A: Using broad and emotional generalizations
options.B: Avoiding any mention of financial costs
options.C: Asking for general moral encouragement
options.D: Requesting specific and measurable steps

explanation: A strong Call to Action leaves no ambiguity about what exact step the decision-maker needs to take next. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T8#GNS124_U4_T8_h4)

question: Which statement is an example of a clear Call to Action for a local health board?

options.A: Let us all work hand in hand to make our primary health centers better
options.B: Approve the purchase of three solar refrigerators for vaccine storage by Friday
options.C: Healthcare is a fundamental human right that deserves our collective attention
options.D: Think about the children in our communities who lack access to vaccines

explanation: This option gives a direct, time-bound, and specific instruction that the health board can vote on or act upon immediately. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T8#GNS124_U4_T8_h4)

question: Which communication channel is most effective for reaching grassroots community members in rural areas?

options.A: Closed-circuit television broadcasts
options.B: International academic medical journals
options.C: Town criers and village square meetings
options.D: Official federal government gazettes

explanation: Traditional grassroots channels like town criers easily reach populations with limited access to print media or the internet. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T8#GNS124_U4_T8_h5)

question: Why must nurses assess local literacy levels when choosing communication media?

options.A: To match the message format with the community's ability to read
options.B: To evaluate the clinical competency of the nursing staff
options.C: To determine the exact budget required for hospital uniforms
options.D: To comply with international nursing research guidelines

explanation: Relying on written pamphlets in low-literacy populations fails to deliver the message, necessitating verbal or visual channels instead. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T8#GNS124_U4_T8_h5)

question: How should a nurse handle counter-arguments from stakeholders who claim there is no money for health?

options.A: Demonstrate how health investments improve economic productivity
options.B: Abandon the advocacy campaign until government revenue increases
options.C: Threaten to report the uncooperative officials to the media
options.D: Insist that health is more important than roads without providing data

explanation: Linking health to broader economic gains helps counter the argument that health spending drains resources from other sectors. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T8#GNS124_U4_T8_h6)

question: What is the main benefit of anticipating pushback before launching an advocacy campaign?

options.A: Preventing the public from asking difficult questions
options.B: Eliminating the need to consult community leaders
options.C: Reducing the overall duration of the project planning
options.D: Building robust, evidence-backed defenses into the pitch

explanation: Preparing for anticipated objections ensures the advocate remains calm, credible, and persuasive during negotiations. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T8#GNS124_U4_T8_h6)

question: What is the best indicator that an advocacy campaign targeting policy change was successful?

options.A: The positive personal feelings of the nursing advocacy team
options.B: An amendment or creation of a relevant health policy or budget line
options.C: The total number of advocacy flyers printed and distributed
options.D: An increase in the number of staff meetings held at the clinic

explanation: The ultimate goal of advocacy is policy or resource change, making official policy amendments the truest measure of success. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T8#GNS124_U4_T8_h7)

question: Why is counting distributed flyers an insufficient measure of true advocacy impact?

options.A: It measures output rather than actual policy or behavioral change
options.B: It is too expensive to track paper distribution numbers accurately
options.C: It only provides data on what opposing stakeholders are doing
options.D: It violates confidentiality agreements with the local government

explanation: Distributing materials shows activity, but evaluation requires knowing if those materials actually influenced decisions or health habits. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T8#GNS124_U4_T8_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of health education?

options.A: Voluntary behavioral change for better health
options.B: Diagnosis of complex community diseases
options.C: Strict enforcement of medical laws
options.D: Distribution of free pharmaceutical drugs

explanation: Health education aims to empower people to change their habits willingly through increased understanding rather than force. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T1#GNS124_U5_T1_h1)

question: Why does explaining the reason behind a health practice improve compliance?

options.A: It bridges the gap between knowledge and actual practice
options.B: It eliminates all cultural beliefs instantly
options.C: It replaces the need for community health workers entirely
options.D: It guarantees immediate funding from the government

explanation: Understanding the underlying cause helps individuals see the personal relevance of adopting a new behavior. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T1#GNS124_U5_T1_h1)

question: A key objective of health education in primary health care is promoting what?

options.A: Total dependence on foreign medical aid
options.B: Centralized control of all hospitals
options.C: Community self-reliance in health management
options.D: Elimination of traditional birth attendants

explanation: Primary health care focuses on building local capacity so communities can handle basic health needs independently. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T1#GNS124_U5_T1_h2)

question: How does health education improve the utilization of primary health facilities?

options.A: By converting health posts into full surgical centers
options.B: By teaching people when and how to seek early care
options.C: By providing free transport vehicles for every household
options.D: By increasing the salary of nurses working in rural clinics

explanation: Educated communities recognize early symptoms and visit clinics promptly instead of waiting for complications. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T1#GNS124_U5_T1_h2)

question: Which principle requires involving the community actively rather than just lecturing?

options.A: Jargon usage
options.B: Participation
options.C: Strict isolation
options.D: Passive listening

explanation: Active participation ensures that learners engage with the material and take ownership of their health actions. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T1#GNS124_U5_T1_h3)

question: Why is addressing seasonal health issues an application of the principle of relevance?

options.A: It matches the current health threats facing the community
options.B: It prevents the government from buying medications
options.C: It reduces the workload of clinic nurses significantly
options.D: It guarantees financial rewards for the educators

explanation: Relevance means teaching about problems people are actively experiencing, such as malaria during the rains. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T1#GNS124_U5_T1_h3)

question: What component of the Health Belief Model refers to a person's belief in their own ability to take action?

options.A: Perceived severity
options.B: Cues to action
options.C: Self-efficacy
options.D: External pressure

explanation: Self-efficacy is the confidence an individual has in successfully performing a recommended health behavior. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T1#GNS124_U5_T1_h4)

question: A pregnant woman refuses to attend antenatal care because the clinic is too far and transport cost is high. Which HBM concept does this represent?

options.A: Cues to action
options.B: Perceived benefits
options.C: Perceived susceptibility
options.D: Perceived barriers

question: Which educational method reaches the largest number of people simultaneously?

options.A: Home visitation
options.B: Mass approach
options.C: Individual counseling
options.D: One-on-one bedside teaching

question: What is the main advantage of using a group approach over a mass approach in rural health education?

options.A: It allows participants to ask questions and discuss freely
options.B: It requires zero preparation from the community nurse
options.C: It guarantees that every single villager will attend
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for visual aids

explanation: Group sessions foster interaction, peer learning, and immediate clarification of doubts. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T1#GNS124_U5_T1_h5)

question: What is the very first step in planning a community health education program?

options.A: Needs assessment
options.B: Selecting a venue
options.C: Buying loud speakers
options.D: Printing certificates

explanation: You must first discover what problems exist before designing educational interventions to solve them. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T1#GNS124_U5_T1_h6)

question: Why must program objectives be measurable during the planning phase?

options.A: To accurately determine if the goals were achieved during evaluation
options.B: To prevent community members from asking difficult questions
options.C: To make the written report look professional and long
options.D: To satisfy strict international funding requirements only

explanation: Measurable objectives give clear criteria to judge whether the intervention was successful. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T1#GNS124_U5_T1_h6)

question: Which factor is NOT a common barrier to health education in resource-limited settings?

options.A: Conflicting cultural or religious beliefs
options.B: Erratic electricity supply for electronic aids

options.D: Excessive availability of trained health educators

question: What type of evaluation is conducted during the actual implementation of a program to make adjustments?

options.A: Financial audit
options.B: Formative evaluation
options.C: Retrospective census

question: Why is measuring changes in health statistics more reliable than simply asking attendees if they enjoyed a lecture?

options.A: It shows actual behavioral impact rather than mere politeness
options.B: It stops people from asking questions about the disease
options.C: It takes less time than handing out evaluation questionnaires
options.D: It proves that the health workers were paid their salaries

question: What is the primary focus of Behaviour Change Communication in health care?

options.C: Conducting laboratory tests in rural clinics
options.D: Promoting positive health behaviours through dialogue

question: How does BCC differ from traditional health education?

options.C: Traditional education requires two-way community dialogue
options.D: BCC addresses cultural beliefs and underlying attitudes

question: A key characteristic of adult learners is that they are generally:

options.B: Self-directed and motivated by practical needs
options.C: Unwilling to question new health concepts

question: Why must nurses incorporate community experiences into adult health sessions?

options.B: It validates local wisdom and builds mutual trust
options.C: It eliminates the need for formal nursing assessments
options.D: It ensures patients memorize textbook definitions

explanation: Adults bring valuable life experience; acknowledging this background prevents resistance and fosters a collaborative learning environment. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T10#GNS124_U5_T10_h2)

question: Which method is commonly used to assess community learning needs?

options.B: Reviewing national budget allocations for health
options.C: Waiting for patients to report to tertiary hospitals
options.D: Reading international medical research journals exclusively

question: A nurse notices poor antenatal clinic attendance despite health talks. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Assess the community for hidden cultural or financial barriers
options.C: Stop providing health education classes altogether

question: What is a major benefit of using drama in community health education?

options.C: It forces community members to memorize complex medical terms
options.D: It replaces the need for any verbal communication

explanation: Drama utilizes familiar cultural forms to convey health messages effectively across diverse literacy levels. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T10#GNS124_U5_T10_h4)

question: Why should nurses avoid relying solely on standard lectures for community health talks?

options.A: Lectures often fail to engage low-literacy or diverse audiences
options.B: Lectures require advanced laboratory equipment
options.C: Lectures are banned in primary health care centers
options.D: Lectures take too much time to prepare beforehand

question: What is the primary purpose of the teach-back method during patient counseling?

options.A: Testing the patient for memory loss conditions
options.B: Confirming that the patient truly understands the instructions
options.C: Evaluating the nurse's public speaking skills
options.D: Complying with hospital billing requirements

question: How does establishing good rapport impact clinical behaviour change communication?

options.A: It guarantees 100 percent medication adherence
options.B: It encourages open dialogue and honest health disclosures
options.C: It eliminates the need for any follow-up visits
options.D: It shortens the consultation time to zero minutes

explanation: Trusting relationships make patients feel safe to discuss sensitive health challenges without fear of judgment. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T10#GNS124_U5_T10_h5)

question: What is the ultimate goal of evaluating a BCC program?

options.A: Punishing communities that fail to learn
options.B: Measuring actual behavioural change and health improvement
options.C: Collecting fees from workshop participants
options.D: Writing academic papers for promotion

explanation: True evaluation focuses on whether health practices and outcomes actually improved following the educational intervention. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T10#GNS124_U5_T10_h6)

question: What should a nurse do if program evaluation shows a failure to adopt healthy behaviors?

options.A: Falsify records to show successful outcomes

question: What is the primary focus of counselling compared to guidance?

options.B: Emotional exploration and behavior change

question: Why is guidance considered broader than counselling?

options.A: It encompasses general information giving and directional advice
options.B: It focuses exclusively on mental illness treatment
options.C: It takes place only inside hospital wards
options.D: It requires a licensed psychiatrist to be performed

question: Which setting is most typical for formal counselling sessions?

options.A: A private, quiet clinical room
options.B: An open community market
options.C: A busy immunization queue
options.D: A crowded hospital corridor

question: How does the approach in counselling differ from guidance?

options.B: Guidance requires specialized psychiatric certification
options.C: Guidance focuses purely on deep emotional trauma

question: What does the principle of confidentiality require a nurse to do?

options.D: Discuss clinical cases with casual friends

question: When is it legally and ethically acceptable to break patient confidentiality?

options.B: When the client threatens harm to self or others
options.C: When a curious neighbor asks about the patient

question: Which type of counselling helps patients adhere to antiretroviral therapy?

options.A: Vocational career guidance

question: A nursing mother is struggling to balance work stress and infant care. What type of counselling is most appropriate?

options.A: Personal and lifestyle counselling
options.B: Industrial engineering advice
options.C: Strictly academic tutoring
options.D: Purely architectural guidance

question: What is the very first stage in a proper counselling process?

options.A: Prescribing heavy sedatives
options.B: Discharging the patient immediately
options.C: Imposing strict behavioral rules
options.D: Building rapport and trust

question: Why is collaborative goal setting important during counselling?

question: Which question type encourages a client to share more detailed feelings?

explanation: Adapting strategies based on local feedback helps overcome resistance and builds sustainable community trust. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T8#GNS124_U5_T8_h8)

question: What does the acronym IEC stand for in public health?

options.A: Immunization, Evaluation, and Care
options.B: Investigation, Epidemiology, and Cure
options.C: Infection, Environment, and Control
options.D: Information, Education, and Communication

explanation: IEC stands for Information, Education, and Communication, representing the core pillars of public health promotion campaigns. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T9#GNS124_U5_T9_h1)

question: Why is two-way communication considered vital within an IEC program?

options.A: It allows health workers to listen to community feedback and address specific concerns.
options.B: It reduces the time spent during routine hospital ward rounds.
options.C: It eliminates the need for written health pamphlets entirely.
options.D: It ensures that patients memorize medical terminology quickly.

explanation: Two-way dialogue ensures community members can ask questions and express doubts, making health messages more relevant and acceptable. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T9#GNS124_U5_T9_h1)

question: True or false: Providing health facts alone guarantees immediate behaviour modification.

options.A: True
options.B: False
options.C: Only in urban areas
options.D: Only during disease outbreaks

explanation: Facts are necessary, but behavioural change is complex and influenced by economic, social, and psychological factors. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T9#GNS124_U5_T9_h2)

question: A patient understands that smoking causes lung cancer but refuses to stop. What does this situation demonstrate?

options.A: Smoking has no actual adverse health effects in practice.
options.B: The primary health clinic lacks adequate medical supplies.
options.C: Knowledge alone is not always enough to trigger immediate behavioural change.
options.D: The patient failed to hear the nurse's initial instructions.

explanation: Patients often require support, skill-building, and motivation beyond mere factual knowledge to overcome addiction or deep-seated habits. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T9#GNS124_U5_T9_h2)

question: Which health model focuses heavily on a person's perceived susceptibility and perceived severity of a disease?

options.A: The Health Belief Model
options.B: The Epidemiological Triad
options.C: The Biomedical Model
options.D: The Germ Theory of Disease

explanation: The Health Belief Model evaluates how an individual's personal beliefs about disease threats influence health-related actions. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T9#GNS124_U5_T9_h3)

question: What is the primary focus of the precontemplation stage in the Stages of Change model?

options.A: The individual does not yet recognize a need to change their behaviour.
options.B: The individual is actively practicing the new health habit daily.
options.C: The individual is planning to visit the clinic tomorrow.
options.D: The individual has completely relapsed into old habits.

explanation: In precontemplation, people are often unaware or unconcerned about their risky behaviours and do not intend to change. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T9#GNS124_U5_T9_h3)

question: Which IEC channel is best suited for direct, two-way dialogue and clearing personal doubts?

options.A: Interpersonal communication
options.B: National television advertisements
options.C: Anonymous radio jingles
options.D: Billboards along major highways

explanation: Interpersonal communication involves direct interaction between the health worker and the client, enabling personalized questions and immediate clarification. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T9#GNS124_U5_T9_h4)

question: Why is a combination of mass media and interpersonal communication recommended for health campaigns?

options.A: Mass media is legally required for all government hospitals in Nigeria.
options.B: Combining both methods prevents patients from asking questions.
options.C: Interpersonal communication is too expensive to use on its own.
options.D: Mass media builds broad awareness while interpersonal communication deepens understanding and motivates action.

explanation: Using multiple channels reinforces the core health message and reaches people through different sensory modalities. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T9#GNS124_U5_T9_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of pre-testing IEC materials with community members?

options.A: To fulfill mandatory international copyright laws
options.B: To calculate the total financial budget for printing
options.C: To test the physical durability of the paper used
options.D: To check for clarity, cultural appropriateness, and potential misunderstandings

explanation: Pre-testing ensures that the target audience understands the message correctly and finds the images and language acceptable. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T9#GNS124_U5_T9_h5)

question: Why must health messages be translated into local languages instead of relying solely on English?

options.A: Many rural community members do not understand or read English fluently.
options.B: Government policy forbids the use of English in primary health centers.
options.C: Local languages make medical treatments work faster in the body.
options.D: English words are too short to fit on standard health posters.

question: Where do nurses typically find everyday opportunities to conduct IEC sessions?

options.A: Antenatal clinics, immunization outreaches, and outpatient departments

options.C: Hospital accounting departments and revenue collection desks
options.D: Administrative boardrooms during budget meetings

question: What is a key attribute that makes a nurse effective as an IEC change agent?

options.A: Building trust and showing empathy during patient interactions

options.D: Strictly using advanced Latin terminology during health talks

question: Which of the following is NOT a common barrier to behavioural change in primary health care?

question: How do harmful traditional practices affect public health IEC campaigns?

options.A: They replace the need for community mobilization altogether.

question: What percentage of diagnostic clues can a thorough client interview typically reveal?

question: Why should a nurse view history taking as more than just administrative data collection?

question: Which communication tool invites broad patient descriptions instead of short answers?

options.A: Rapid interrogation prompts

options.C: Interrupt immediately with a direct medical question

question: What is the very first step in organizing a proper patient interview?

question: Why is following a structured interview format essential for student nurses?

options.A: Color

question: What is the primary purpose of a physical examination in clinical practice?

question: Why must a nurse verify patient identity using two identifiers before collecting a laboratory specimen?

question: Why should a nurse evaluate a laboratory result within the context of the patient's clinical state?

question: A patient's lab report shows a critically high potassium level. What immediate action should the nurse take?

question: Which practice directly prevents needle-stick injuries during diagnostic specimen collection?

question: What is the main purpose of quality assurance programs in diagnostic testing?

question: What does the letter 'A' stand for in the ABCD framework of nutritional assessment?

question: Why is early nutritional assessment important in primary health care settings?

question: What is the main use of a Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) tape?

question: A nurse divides a patient's weight in kilograms by height in meters squared. What is being calculated?

question: Which deficiency is shown by the presence of Bitot's spots on the eyes?

question: Why do nurses check tissues with rapid cell turnover during a nutritional assessment?

question: What does a serum hemoglobin test primarily help screen for?

options.A: Iron-deficiency anemia
options.B: Acute protein loss

options.D: Electrolyte imbalance

question: What is a major limitation of relying only on a 24-hour dietary recall?

options.A: It measures long-term nutrient storage over several years

options.C: It depends entirely on the patient's memory and honesty

question: Why must nurses look at socio-economic factors during a nutritional assessment?

options.A: Economic status dictates the exact metabolic rate of an individual

question: What is the term for the period of seasonal food scarcity that happens before a new harvest?

options.A: The fiscal quarter

question: A nurse combines anthropometric, clinical, and dietary data to create what?

question: Why is it important to use locally available foods when giving dietary advice to patients?

question: What is the main purpose of a standing order in primary health care?

options.A: Allowing nurses to treat specific conditions without direct doctor consultation
options.B: Replacing all hospital physicians with community health workers
options.C: Permitting nurses to prescribe any restricted medication independently
options.D: Providing administrative guidelines for hospital financial management

explanation: Standing orders provide pre-approved clinical authorization so nurses can initiate care for common conditions without waiting for a physician. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T6#GNS124_U6_T6_h1)

question: Why are standing orders very important in rural Nigerian primary health clinics?

options.C: They compensate for low doctor-to-patient ratios in remote areas

explanation: Rural clinics frequently lack resident physicians, making protocols essential for timely frontline clinical decision-making. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T6#GNS124_U6_T6_h1)

question: Who is legally responsible when a nurse executes a standing order incorrectly?

options.A: The executing nurse who performed the clinical assessment
options.B: The pharmaceutical company that manufactured the drug
options.C: The patient who consented to the treatment
options.D: The national health minister exclusively

explanation: The clinician carrying out the protocol remains personally accountable for their assessment and application of the standing order. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T6#GNS124_U6_T6_h2)

question: What should a nurse do when a patient has symptoms not covered by an existing standing order?

options.A: Modify the standing order to fit the patient's symptoms
options.B: Proceed with treatment using personal clinical guesswork
options.C: Discharge the patient without any further intervention
options.D: Seek medical guidance or refer the patient upward

explanation: Protocols cannot cover every rare complication, so exceeding their boundaries requires direct medical consultation or referral. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T6#GNS124_U6_T6_h2)

question: What is the first step a nurse must take before using any standing order?

options.A: Write a prescription for a specialist referral
options.B: Notify the state health commissioner immediately

options.D: Perform a systematic patient assessment and take vital signs

explanation: A baseline assessment is mandatory to confirm that the patient's presentation matches the specific criteria of the protocol. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T6#GNS124_U6_T6_h3)

question: A patient meets all requirements for a malaria standing order except for a known allergy to the drug. What is the correct action?

options.C: Administer the drug anyway since the protocol is approved
options.D: Do NOT use the standing order and seek medical review

question: Which condition is commonly managed using standard primary health care protocols in Nigeria?

options.B: Advanced chronic kidney disease
options.C: Uncomplicated malaria
options.D: Open-heart surgery recovery

question: Why are complex surgical procedures absent from standard primary health care standing orders?

options.C: Patients with surgical needs never visit primary health clinics
options.D: Protocols only apply to preventive medicine and immunizations

question: What must be easily reachable when giving medications via standing orders that carry allergy risks?

question: How are medication dosages usually decided within primary health care standing orders?

options.B: Randomized selection by the attending nurse

question: What is the legal consequence of failing to document care provided through a standing order?

question: Why does public health tracking rely on proper documentation of standing order usage?

options.A: To restrict patient access to essential health services

question: What must a nurse do when a patient's condition shows emergency warning signs during protocol treatment?

question: Why is a written referral note critical when transferring a patient to a larger hospital?

question: What is the purpose of conducting regular clinical checks on standing order usage?

question: Why must standing orders be updated when national health treatment guidelines change?

question: What is the primary purpose of public health surveillance in primary health care?

question: What is the primary purpose of establishing clear referral pathways in primary health care?

question: What is the primary goal of health education in primary health care?

question: Which of these is a major health challenge that Nigerian nurses frequently encounter in the community?

question: Why should a nurse study local disease patterns before planning a health talk?

question: A nurse is teaching mothers about ORS preparation. Instead of just lecturing, she asks a mother to come forward and mix the solution herself. Which learning principle is the nurse using?

question: What is the primary benefit of involving local community leaders when planning a health education program?

question: Why should a nurse check local market days and religious schedules before setting a date for a community health talk?

question: Why should nurses avoid using heavy medical jargon when teaching community members?

question: What is the best way for a nurse to respond when a client shares a traditional belief that goes against medical science?

question: Which of these is NOT a common barrier to changing health behaviors in a community?

question: What is the main purpose of evaluating a community health education program?

question: Why do children in rural areas often catch the heaviest parasite loads of schistosomiasis?

options.B: Their immune systems are genetically unable to fight blood flukes.
options.C: They spend more time swimming and playing in infested water.
options.D: Their diets lack the necessary proteins to resist parasite invasion.

explanation: Kids love to swim and play in rivers! Because they spend so much time in the water, they are exposed more often to the tiny parasites looking for a host. Makes total sense, right? [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h1)

question: Which stage of the schistosome life cycle can directly infect humans?

options.A: Sporocysts
options.B: Miracidia
options.C: Cercariae
options.D: Eggs

explanation: Cercariae are the free-swimming little swimmers released by snails into the water. When they touch human skin, they dive right in! You've got this. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h2)

question: What is the main job of freshwater snails in the life cycle of schistosomes?

options.A: They transport the parasite permanently out of aquatic environments.
options.B: They consume human waste to reduce overall environmental egg counts.
options.C: They serve as the definitive host where adult worms reproduce sexually.
options.D: They act as intermediate hosts where asexual multiplication occurs.

explanation: Think of the snail as a busy factory! Inside the snail, a single parasite multiplies into thousands of infectious cercariae. Neat biology fact for your clinical notes! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h2)

question: How does the schistosomiasis parasite usually get into the human body?

options.A: Skin penetration by cercariae in contaminated water
options.B: Inhalation of airborne dust near infected rivers
options.C: Ingestion of poorly cooked freshwater fish
options.D: Bites from infected mosquitoes near stagnant pools

explanation: The parasite doesn't wait to be swallowed—it swims right through healthy, unbroken skin when someone wades or swims in an infected stream. Keep up the great studying! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h3)

question: A patient asks if boiling drinking water will fully protect their family from schistosomiasis. As a nurse, what is your best reply?

options.A: Yes, but you also need to avoid skin contact with river water during washing or swimming.
options.B: No, boiling water does nothing because the parasites are only caught by eating raw fish.
options.C: No, you must chemically treat the water with chlorine tablets to kill the snail eggs.
options.D: Yes, because the disease is spread exclusively by drinking unboiled water from streams.

explanation: While drinking clean water is always smart, skin contact is the main trap here! Bathing or washing clothes in infested streams is how most people catch it. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h3)

question: What is a classic sign of chronic urinary schistosomiasis?

options.A: Severe chest pain
options.B: Terminal hematuria
options.C: Swollen painful joints
options.D: Jaundice and yellow eyes

explanation: As trapped parasite eggs irritate the bladder lining, blood shows up right at the very end of passing urine (terminal hematuria). A classic nursing assessment sign! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h4)

question: What causes the sudden symptoms of Katayama fever (acute schistosomiasis)?

options.A: The immediate accumulation of snail toxins inside the human bloodstream
options.B: A secondary bacterial infection entering through skin puncture sites
options.C: The migration and development of immature worms through tissues
options.D: The sudden death of adult worms inside the intestinal lumen

explanation: Katayama fever is basically your immune system throwing a fit as young worms travel through your body tissues and blood. Your body is fighting hard! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h4)

question: What is the standard lab test used to check for urinary schistosomiasis?

options.A: Blood culture to isolate active bacterial colonies
options.B: Urine microscopy using filtration to find eggs
options.C: Chest X-ray to visualize lung calcifications
options.D: Liver biopsy to inspect adult worm clusters

explanation: By filtering a urine sample, lab technicians can catch the tiny parasite eggs under a microscope. Simple, non-invasive, and effective! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h5)

question: Why might a patient's stool or urine test show a false negative early in a schistosomiasis infection?

options.A: The eggs dissolve immediately in fresh urine or stool samples.
options.B: The parasites hide inside bone marrow where tests cannot reach.
options.C: Eosinophils in the blood destroy all eggs before they reach excretory organs.
options.D: Adult worms have not yet matured and begun laying eggs.

explanation: Tests look for eggs. If the infection is brand new, the worms are still growing up and haven't started laying eggs yet! Always good to keep repeat testing in mind. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h5)

question: What is the frontline medication used to treat schistosomiasis?

options.A: Albendazole
options.B: Metronidazole
options.C: Praziquantel
options.D: Artemether

explanation: Praziquantel is the trusty, WHO-recommended drug used worldwide to clear up this infection. Bookmark this drug name—you'll see it often in exams! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h6)

question: What is a key piece of advice to give a patient who just received praziquantel treatment?

options.A: You must complete a strict 14-day course of tablets to ensure the larvae in your skin die.
options.B: The drug kills adult worms, but you can still get infected again if you swim in contaminated streams.
options.C: You should take the pills on an empty stomach to prevent the drug from dissolving too quickly.
options.D: The medication will immediately reverse any scar tissue already formed in your bladder.

explanation: Praziquantel wipes out the worms currently inside, but it doesn't give you superpowers against future infections. Patient education is our superpower as nurses! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h6)

question: Which long-term health problem is strongly linked to long-term Schistosoma haematobium infection?

options.A: Bladder cancer
options.B: Bone marrow depression
options.C: Lung failure
options.D: Gastric ulcers

explanation: Years of chronic irritation in the bladder from trapped eggs can unfortunately lead to cellular changes and bladder cancer. Another great reason why early treatment matters so much! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h7)

question: How does long-term intestinal schistosomiasis end up causing portal hypertension?

options.A: Adult worms multiply rapidly inside the heart and increase overall blood pressure.
options.B: Intestinal bleeding drains blood volume, forcing the heart to pump at a dangerous rate.
options.C: The kidneys fail to filter salt, causing fluid overload throughout the entire body.
options.D: Trapped eggs cause liver fibrosis that blocks blood flow through the portal vein system.

explanation: When eggs get trapped in the liver, the body forms scar tissue (fibrosis). This traffic jam blocks normal blood flow, raising pressure in the portal vein. Pathophysiology made clear! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h7)

question: What is the main public health approach used to control schistosomiasis in heavily affected communities?

options.A: Widespread daily chlorine spraying of all farmlands
options.B: Mandatory quarantine of all infected families
options.C: Mass drug administration of praziquantel
options.D: Surgical removal of adult worms from patients

explanation: Instead of waiting for individuals to fall sick, health teams treat whole communities—especially school children—all at once to knock down the disease burden. Brilliant public health strategy! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h8)

question: A community health nurse is planning a schistosomiasis prevention program in a rural Nigerian village. Which action will provide the most lasting protection?

options.A: Installing clean, accessible piped water and functional sanitation toilets
options.B: Providing free malaria mosquito nets to every household in the village
options.C: Instructing villagers to boil all river water before using it for cooking
options.D: Giving nutritional supplements to adults to boost their body weight

explanation: Clean tap water and proper toilets mean villagers won't need to step into infected streams or contaminate the water sources. That's how we solve the root cause! You're thinking like a true nurse. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h8)

question: Which animal is known as the natural reservoir host for the Ebola virus?

options.A: Pigs on farms
options.B: Domestic dogs
options.C: Fruit bats
options.D: Cattle and goats

explanation: Spot on! Fruit bats carry the virus naturally without getting sick themselves. Think of them as the original home of the virus in nature. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h1)

question: Why do we call Ebola a zoonotic disease?

options.A: It spreads exclusively among wild animals in the forest
options.B: It can only be transmitted through contaminated water
options.C: It mutates rapidly inside human respiratory tracts
options.D: It originates in animals and spreads to humans

explanation: You got it! 'Zoonotic' simply means an infection that jumps from animals to humans. Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h1)

question: When the Ebola virus enters the human body, which immune cells does it attack first?

options.A: Red blood cells and platelets
options.B: Epithelial cells of the skin
options.C: Macrophages and monocytes
options.D: Neuron cells in the brain

explanation: Spot on! The virus tricks our body by attacking our own defense cells (macrophages and monocytes) right from the start. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h2)

question: A community health nurse is teaching villagers how Ebola spreads. Which practice should she warn against the most?

options.A: Drinking boiled water from a community well during dry seasons
options.B: Eating well-cooked pork from certified local livestock farms
options.C: Washing the body of a relative who died from suspected Ebola
options.D: Sharing eating utensils with a family member who has malaria

explanation: Well done! The viral load is super high in someone who just passed away, making traditional burial touching very risky. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h2)

question: What is the usual incubation period range for Ebola?

options.A: 2 to 21 days
options.B: 1 to 3 hours
options.C: 6 months to a year
options.D: 30 to 60 days

explanation: Correct! Symptoms can show up anywhere from 2 days to 3 weeks after contact. That's why monitoring takes up to 21 days. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h3)

question: Which signs and symptoms usually show up first when a person is coming down with Ebola?

options.A: Sudden fever, fatigue, and severe muscle aches
options.B: Profuse internal bleeding and skin bruising
options.C: Paralysis of the lower limbs and blindness
options.D: Productive cough and severe chest congestion

explanation: You nailed it! Early Ebola can easily feel like malaria or typhoid at first—sudden fever and body weakness are the major clues. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h3)

question: Why is it so important to quickly isolate a suspected Ebola patient in a clinic?

options.A: It allows the lab to make local drugs
options.B: It prevents the virus from spreading to other patients and healthcare staff
options.C: It eliminates the need to wear protective gowns
options.D: It cures the patient before bleeding starts

explanation: Spot on! Isolating patients cuts off the transmission chain immediately and keeps everyone else in the ward safe. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h4)

question: What is the gold-standard laboratory test used to confirm an Ebola infection?

options.A: Routine microscopic examination of red blood cells
options.B: X-ray imaging of the chest
options.C: Stool microscopy for parasites
options.D: Reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR)

explanation: Correct! RT-PCR is the reliable test that catches the virus's RNA in blood samples. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h4)

question: What is the main focus of nursing care for a patient with Ebola?

options.A: Administering high-dose broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.B: Placing the patient on complete bed rest without food or water
options.C: Providing supportive care like fluid replacement and symptom relief
options.D: Surgically removing infected lymph nodes

explanation: You got it! Since it's a virus, nursing care is all about keeping the patient hydrated and comfortable while their immune system fights. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h5)

question: An Ebola patient is vomiting and having terrible watery diarrhea. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.A: Stop all oral meds until diarrhea clears up
options.B: Start aggressive rehydration therapy to correct fluid and electrolyte losses
options.C: Restrict all oral fluids to give the tummy a rest
options.D: Apply warm compresses to stop belly cramps

explanation: Spot on! Replacing lost fluids quickly is lifesaving because dehydration and shock are the big dangers here. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h5)

question: Which part of wearing Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) is most risky for accidentally contaminating yourself?

options.A: Donning (putting on) the clean gear
options.B: Storing unused aprons
options.C: Doffing (removing) the contaminated gear
options.D: Walking through the hallway

explanation: Correct! Taking off dirty gear takes the most care because you might accidentally touch germs on the outside. Always follow the steps carefully! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h6)

question: Which of these is a BIG NO-ROUTINE in infection control during an Ebola outbreak?

options.A: Decontaminating room surfaces with chlorine solutions
options.B: Reusing disposable gloves after washing them with ordinary soap
options.C: Limiting the number of staff entering the isolation zone
options.D: Using a trained buddy to watch you remove your PPE

explanation: You got it! Disposable gloves are strictly one-time-use. Never wash and reuse them—safety first! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h6)

question: How long must close contacts of an Ebola patient be watched for signs of illness?

options.A: 5 days
options.B: 3 months
options.C: 48 hours
options.D: 21 days

explanation: Spot on! Since the incubation period is up to 21 days, we keep track of contacts for that full period to catch any early signs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h7)

question: Why is building trust with the community so vital during an Ebola outbreak?

options.A: It stops the virus from becoming airborne
options.B: It lets the government cancel travel bans
options.C: It prevents families from hiding sick relatives and encourages early reporting
options.D: It gives clinic staff higher pay

explanation: Correct! When people trust health workers, they bring sick family members in early instead of hiding them, which stops the spread. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h7)

question: What do we mean by Post-Ebola Syndrome?

options.A: A collection of chronic physical symptoms persisting after recovery
options.B: A permanent mental illness from the incubation period
options.C: An acute respiratory infection before fever starts
options.D: A sudden relapse of active internal bleeding on day two

explanation: You got it! Even after beating the virus, survivors can deal with lingering joint pain, fatigue, and vision issues. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h8)

question: What crucial advice must a nurse give to a male patient who has just recovered from Ebola?

options.A: Return to the isolation ward immediately for another vaccine
options.B: Use barrier contraception or practice safe sex because the virus can linger in semen
options.C: Take daily antibiotics to clear the virus from your joints
options.D: Avoid all physical contact with family forever

explanation: Spot on! The virus can hide in certain body fluids long after recovery, so safe sex guidance is a must for male survivors. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h8)

question: What is the main virus that causes COVID-19?

options.A: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
options.B: SARS-CoV-2
options.C: Influenza A virus
options.D: Respiratory Syncytial Virus

explanation: COVID-19 stands for coronavirus disease 2019, and it is caused by the specific virus called Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). You've got this! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h1)

question: Which part of the COVID-19 virus helps it attach to human cells?

options.A: Lipid capsules
options.B: Peptidoglycan walls
options.C: Flagella tails
options.D: Spike proteins

explanation: Think of the spike proteins as tiny crowns on the outside of the virus that latch onto human cells to start an infection. Great job! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h1)

question: Which human cell receptors does SARS-CoV-2 mainly latch onto?

options.A: Cholinergic receptors
options.B: Insulin receptors
options.C: ACE2 receptors
options.D: Beta-adrenergic receptors

explanation: ACE2 receptors are found in large amounts in our lung tissue, making them the main doorway for the virus to enter the body. Keep it up! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h2)

question: What is the main danger of a cytokine storm in severe COVID-19 patients?

options.A: A sudden drop in core body temperature
options.B: Severe tissue damage from a hyperactive immune response
options.C: Permanent loss of the sense of taste and smell
options.D: Complete shut down of bone marrow white blood cell production

explanation: A cytokine storm happens when the immune system goes into overdrive, flooding the lungs with chemicals that end up harming healthy tissue. You're learning fast! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h2)

question: Which symptom is uniquely linked to COVID-19 compared to many other common respiratory infections?

options.A: Loss of taste or smell
options.B: Yellow skin discoloration
options.C: Uncontrollable muscle spasms
options.D: Severe joint stiffness

explanation: While many bugs give you a cough and fever, suddenly losing your sense of taste or smell is a classic sign of COVID-19. Well spotted! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h3)

question: A patient has a breathing rate of 32 breaths per minute and an oxygen level of 91% on room air. How is this classified?

options.A: Asymptomatic infection
options.B: Mild illness
options.C: Severe illness
options.D: Moderate illness

explanation: An oxygen level below 94% along with fast breathing means the patient is struggling and needs urgent care. You can totally master this! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h3)

question: Why do hospitals immediately isolate patients showing respiratory symptoms?

options.A: To speed up the administration of intravenous fluids
options.B: To reduce the cost of diagnostic testing supplies
options.C: To prevent transmission to staff and other patients
options.D: To allow patients to sleep without hospital noise

explanation: Isolating patients right away stops airborne droplets from spreading to other vulnerable people in the clinic. Smart nursing practice! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h4)

question: What does 'silent hypoxia' mean in COVID-19 patients?

options.A: A complete absence of lung sounds during stethoscope auscultation
options.B: Normal breathing rates paired with severe panic attacks
options.C: Elevated carbon dioxide levels despite normal oxygen saturation
options.D: Dangerously low blood oxygen levels without the feeling of breathlessness

explanation: Some patients have critically low oxygen on monitors yet feel completely fine, which can be tricky and dangerous. Good to know for clinicals! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h4)

question: Why are awake COVID-19 patients sometimes asked to lie on their stomachs (prone positioning)?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for oxygen therapy
options.B: It makes it easier to insert nasogastric feeding tubes
options.C: It improves lung expansion and oxygen exchange
options.D: It prevents patients from developing pressure ulcers

explanation: Proning helps open up parts of the lungs that usually get squished, helping the patient breathe much better. Every day you're building clinical skills! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h5)

question: What type of medicine is often given to hospitalized COVID-19 patients to prevent blood clots?

options.A: Anticoagulants
options.B: Antipyretics
options.C: Antihistamines
options.D: Antibiotics

explanation: COVID-19 can make the blood more likely to clot, so doctors routinely prescribe blood thinners (anticoagulants) to keep patients safe. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h5)

question: What do we call health issues that linger for weeks or months after recovering from COVID-19?

options.A: Acute rebound syndrome
options.B: Secondary convalescence
options.C: Long COVID
options.D: Delayed viral shedding

explanation: When symptoms stick around long after the initial infection is gone, it's known as Long COVID. You're making steady progress! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which of these is a very common complaint from people dealing with Long COVID?

options.A: Chronic fatigue and brain fog
options.B: Permanent paralysis of the lower limbs
options.C: Uncontrollable weight gain within days
options.D: Total loss of long-term childhood memories

explanation: Many patients struggle with extreme tiredness and trouble focusing long after testing negative. Keep up the good work! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which mask must nurses wear during procedures that generate aerosols on COVID-19 patients?

options.A: Plastic face shield alone
options.B: Cloth face covering
options.C: Standard paper surgical mask
options.D: N95 respirator

explanation: Procedures that kick tiny droplets into the air require a tight-fitting N95 mask to keep you safe. Safety first in nursing! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h7)

question: Which of these actions is WRONG when trying to stop the spread of respiratory viruses in a hospital?

options.A: Reusing disposable single-use gloves between multiple patients
options.B: Ensuring proper room ventilation in clinical spaces
options.C: Performing hand hygiene before and after patient contact
options.D: Cleaning high-touch environmental surfaces regularly

explanation: Single-use gloves are meant for one patient only! Reusing them is a sure way to spread germs around. You'd never make that mistake! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h7)

question: What is the main goal of getting widespread COVID-19 vaccinations?

options.A: Prevention of all future bacterial lung infections
options.B: Prevention of severe disease, hospitalization, and death
options.C: Complete eradication of all human coronaviruses worldwide
options.D: Immediate elimination of the need for hand washing

explanation: Vaccines help train your immune system so that even if you catch the virus, you are much less likely to get severely sick or end up in the hospital. Brilliant! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h8)

question: How should a nurse best handle a patient who is hesitant about taking a vaccine?

options.A: Use empathetic communication and provide clear, factual information
options.B: Insist that vaccination is mandatory without discussion
options.C: Ignore their concerns and focus only on willing patients
options.D: Warn them that refusal will result in legal penalties

explanation: Listening patiently and addressing fears with kindness and facts is the best way to build trust. Great nursing communication! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h8)

question: What is the primary physiological defect in Type 1 diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
options.B: Peripheral resistance to the action of insulin
options.C: Temporary glucose intolerance during pregnancy
options.D: Excessive production of glucagon by the liver

explanation: Type 1 diabetes occurs when the immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h1)

question: Why does hyperglycemia occur in patients with diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Dietary protein is converted directly into simple sugars
options.B: Cells fail to absorb glucose due to insulin problems
options.C: The kidneys actively produce excess glucose from water
options.D: The liver stores too much glycogen and refuses to release it

explanation: Without enough effective insulin, glucose cannot enter body cells for energy and instead stays building up in the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h1)

question: What does the term polyuria mean in a patient with diabetes?

options.A: Severe pain and burning sensation during urination
options.B: Excessive production and passing of urine
options.C: A sudden and total inability to pass any urine
options.D: An intense, constant craving for sweet foods

explanation: Polyuria refers to passing large volumes of urine, which happens when excess sugar pulls extra water out of the body. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h2)

question: A patient comes to the clinic complaining of constant thirst, frequent urination, and sudden weight loss. What condition should the nurse suspect first?

options.A: Chronic kidney disease
options.B: Diabetes mellitus
options.C: Urinary tract infection
options.D: Iron deficiency anemia

explanation: The classic trio of excessive thirst, frequent urination, and unexplained weight loss strongly points toward new-onset diabetes mellitus. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h2)

question: What does an HbA1c test measure in a patient with diabetes?

options.A: How well the kidneys are filtering waste products from blood
options.B: The exact amount of insulin currently stored in the liver
options.C: Average blood sugar levels over the past three months
options.D: Immediate blood glucose level at the exact time of the test

explanation: HbA1c measures glucose attached to hemoglobin red blood cells, reflecting average control over their lifespan of about three months. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h3)

question: Why is self-monitoring of blood glucose important for a patient managing diabetes?

options.A: It cures the underlying insulin resistance in Type 2 diabetes
options.B: It helps track daily blood sugar patterns and guide safe care
options.C: It prevents the patient from ever experiencing low blood sugar
options.D: It completely replaces the need for clinic check-ups and lab tests

explanation: Checking blood sugar at home gives immediate feedback on how food, activity, and medicine affect glucose levels day-to-day. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h3)

question: Which medication is typically prescribed as the first-line oral treatment for Type 2 diabetes?

options.A: Regular insulin
options.B: NPH insulin
options.C: Metformin
options.D: Glibenclamide

explanation: Metformin is universally recommended as the starting oral drug because it lowers blood sugar effectively without causing weight gain or low blood sugar on its own. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h4)

question: Why must nurses instruct patients on insulin therapy to rotate their injection sites?

options.A: To make sure the injection needle stays sharp for every single dose
options.B: To prevent abnormal fatty lumps or tissue damage under the skin
options.C: To speed up the onset time of long-acting insulin preparations
options.D: To ensure the insulin is absorbed directly into the stomach lining

explanation: Injecting in the exact same spot repeatedly causes lipodystrophy, which ruins skin tissue and alters how evenly insulin is absorbed. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h4)

question: How does regular physical activity benefit a patient with Type 2 diabetes?

options.A: It helps body cells respond better to available insulin
options.B: It allows the patient to eat unlimited amounts of sugar
options.C: It permanently repairs destroyed cells inside the pancreas
options.D: It replaces the daily need for checking blood sugar levels

explanation: Exercise makes muscle and tissue cells more sensitive to insulin, allowing glucose to move out of the blood and into cells more easily. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h5)

question: What dietary advice is most appropriate for a nurse to give a patient managing Type 2 diabetes?

options.A: Eliminate all forms of carbohydrates completely from the diet
options.B: Rely entirely on fruit juices for daily hydration and energy
options.C: Choose high-fiber foods and practice moderate portion control
options.D: Eat only once a day to keep blood sugar levels completely flat

explanation: Balanced nutrition focuses on whole grains, fiber, and sensible portions rather than dangerous elimination diets. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h5)

question: Which of the following is an acute complication of diabetes caused by dangerously low blood sugar?

options.A: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.B: Diabetic retinopathy
options.C: Peripheral neuropathy
options.D: Hypoglycemia

explanation: Hypoglycemia happens when blood glucose drops too low, triggering symptoms like shaking, sweating, and confusion that require quick treatment. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h6)

question: Why are patients with long-term diabetes at high risk for foot ulcers and amputations?

options.A: Nerve damage and poor blood flow reduce feeling and healing
options.B: Daily physical exercise wears down the bones in the lower legs
options.C: High blood sugar makes the skin on the feet extremely fragile
options.D: Patients naturally lose interest in cleaning and drying their feet

explanation: Neuropathy prevents patients from feeling minor injuries, while poor circulation stops those injuries from healing properly, leading to severe ulcers. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of patient education in diabetes management?

options.A: To ensure the patient memorizes complex medical terminology
options.B: To shift all responsibilities of treatment onto family members
options.C: To empower the patient to safely manage their daily care
options.D: To eliminate the need for any follow-up visits at the clinic

explanation: Since diabetes is a daily home-managed condition, education equips patients with the skills needed to make safe lifestyle and treatment decisions. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h7)

question: How do community support groups help individuals living with diabetes?

options.A: By supplying free prescription medications to every attendee
options.B: By reducing isolation and sharing practical coping strategies
options.C: By diagnosing new medical complications before doctors do
options.D: By replacing professional nursing care with traditional remedies

explanation: Support groups offer emotional encouragement and practical advice from peers who truly understand the daily realities of living with a chronic illness. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h7)

question: What does the systolic blood pressure reading measure?

options.A: The pressure when the heart rests
options.B: The total volume of blood in the body
options.C: The pressure when the heart beats
options.D: The speed of blood flow in veins

explanation: Systolic pressure represents the force in the arteries when the heart muscle contracts to pump blood forward. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h1)

question: Why don't we diagnose someone with high blood pressure (hypertension) after just one high reading?

options.A: Nigerian guidelines require at least five months of tracking
options.B: Blood pressure machines only work accurately on the third try
options.C: Systolic pressure changes constantly based on what food was eaten
options.D: Temporary factors like stress or rushing can falsely raise readings

explanation: Things like rushing to the clinic, traffic anxiety, or pain can make BP jump temporarily. That's why we always check a few times before making a diagnosis. Great job thinking like a nurse! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h1)

question: Primary hypertension is also frequently called what?

options.A: Secondary hypertension
options.B: Gestational hypertension
options.C: Reversible hypertension
options.D: Essential hypertension

explanation: We call it 'essential hypertension' when high blood pressure happens on its own without another clear medical condition causing it. Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h2)

question: Which of the following is a modifiable risk factor for hypertension?

options.A: Family genetic history
options.B: Chronological aging
options.C: Biological sex
options.D: High dietary salt intake

explanation: Modifiable risk factors are lifestyle habits or conditions that a person can change, such as reducing salt intake, unlike age or genetics. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h2)

question: Why is hypertension frequently called the 'silent killer'?

options.A: It usually causes no symptoms in its early stages
options.B: Patients refuse to talk about their diagnosis
options.C: It stops the heart without any warning sounds
options.D: It only affects people who are sleeping

explanation: Because high blood pressure rarely causes physical discomfort initially, individuals often remain unaware of their condition until complications arise. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h3)

question: If a patient has severe hypertension, which symptom might they complain about?

options.A: Severe pain in the lower abdomen
options.B: Morning occipital headaches
options.C: Sudden swelling in both feet
options.D: Uncontrolled trembling of hands

explanation: A pounding headache right at the back of the head (occipital area) when waking up is a classic warning sign of very high pressure. Keep storing these clinical pearls! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h3)

question: What happens to a patient's blood pressure reading if you use a cuff that is too small for their arm?

options.A: The blood pressure reading will be falsely low
options.B: The mercury column will fail to rise at all
options.C: The reading will remain completely normal
options.D: The blood pressure reading will be falsely high

explanation: A tiny cuff squeezes too hard against a big arm, making the reading look much higher than it really is. Always match your cuff size to the patient! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h4)

question: How long should a patient sit quietly before you measure their blood pressure?

options.A: No rest time is needed
options.B: At least thirty minutes
options.C: At least five minutes
options.D: Exactly one hour

explanation: Giving them 5 minutes to sit and breathe lets walking, talking, or anxiety settle so you get an accurate baseline reading. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h4)

question: What is the main goal of the DASH diet for someone with high blood pressure?

options.A: To increase potassium, calcium, and fiber while reducing sodium
options.B: To replace all fluid intake with specialized herbal teas
options.C: To encourage rapid weight loss through strict calorie counting
options.D: To eliminate all carbohydrates from the daily meal plan

explanation: DASH focuses on whole foods packed with good minerals like potassium and calcium while cutting back on salt to protect the heart. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a good lifestyle change for managing high blood pressure?

options.A: Engaging in regular aerobic exercise
options.B: Increasing dietary sodium intake
options.C: Stopping tobacco smoking completely
options.D: Limiting heavy alcohol consumption

explanation: More salt (sodium) holds onto water in the body and pushes blood pressure up—definitely something we want patients to cut back on! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h5)

question: A patient says, 'My BP is normal today, so I'll stop my drugs.' What is the best way for a nurse to reply?

options.A: Suggest replacing the prescribed drugs with local palm wine
options.B: Agree that normal readings mean the disease has gone away permanently
options.C: Tell the patient to double the dose whenever they feel dizzy
options.D: Explain that the medication controls the condition rather than curing it

explanation: Normal readings just mean the medication is doing its job! Stopping it will cause the pressure to shoot right back up. Patient education is key! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h6)

question: What does the term 'orthostatic hypotension' mean?

options.A: A sudden drop in blood pressure when standing up
options.B: Swelling in the lower legs due to poor circulation
options.C: A spike in heart rate after eating heavy meals
options.D: High blood pressure caused by sleeping flat on the back

explanation: When blood vessels are slow to adjust to a new position, standing up too fast can cause a dizzy spell because of a sudden drop in pressure. Good to know for patient safety! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h6)

question: What is the main difference between hypertensive urgency and a hypertensive emergency?

options.A: Whether the patient is male or female
options.B: The time of day the blood pressure was checked
options.C: The exact numerical value of the diastolic reading
options.D: The presence of acute target organ damage

explanation: Urgency means extremely high pressure, but emergency means the high pressure is actively harming vital organs like the heart or brain. Big difference in how fast we act! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h7)
