question: A patient arrives at the clinic with a BP of 220/130 mmHg, chest pain, and confusion. What are they likely experiencing?

options.A: Normal white coat syndrome
options.B: Isolated systolic hypertension
options.C: Hypertensive urgency
options.D: Hypertensive emergency

explanation: Extremely high blood pressure plus signs of brain or heart distress (like confusion and chest pain) makes this a critical medical emergency. You're crushing these clinical scenarios! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h7)

question: What is the main thing that makes cancer cells different from normal body cells?

options.A: Growing and spreading without normal body control
options.B: Destroying tissues only when bacteria are present
options.C: Stopping all cell division permanently
options.D: Sudden shrinkage of major organs

explanation: Think of normal cells as following strict traffic rules, while cancer cells throw out the rulebook and multiply uncontrollably. You've got this! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h1)

question: Why is it super important for nurses in primary health clinics to know about cancer?

options.A: Primary health centers run all national chemotherapy programs
options.B: Infectious diseases are no longer treated in Nigeria
options.C: Community clinics handle complex surgeries daily
options.D: Nurses are usually the first health workers patients see with early symptoms

explanation: Spotting early signs at the grass-roots level means we can refer patients quickly and save lives. Great nursing starts in the community! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h1)

question: What do we call the process when cancer cells break away and travel to other parts of the body?

options.A: Apoptosis
options.B: Hyperplasia
options.C: Metastasis
options.D: Initiation

explanation: Metastasis is just the medical term for cancer packing its bags and traveling through the blood or lymph to start a new tumor elsewhere. You're mastering the terms! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h2)

question: What actually happens during the 'promotion' stage of cancer development?

options.A: Mutated cells are stimulated to divide over and over
options.B: Cancer cells immediately travel to the brain
options.C: All abnormal cells safely destroy themselves
options.D: Normal DNA is completely repaired by enzymes

explanation: During promotion, things like lifestyle factors or irritants encourage those already-changed cells to keep multiplying into a bigger problem. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h2)

question: Which common virus is strongly linked to the development of cervical cancer?

options.A: Human Immunodeficiency Virus
options.B: Human Papillomavirus
options.C: Epstein-Barr virus
options.D: Hepatitis B virus

explanation: High-risk strains of HPV can cause changes in cervical cells over time. This is why screening and the HPV vaccine are such big wins in public health! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h3)

question: A 45-year-old woman comes to the clinic with a hard, painless breast lump she noticed six months ago. What often causes this kind of late presentation in our communities?

options.A: Cultural stigma and trying alternative therapies first
options.B: The lump grew instantly overnight
options.C: Routine mammograms are done everywhere
options.D: The tumor was already surgically removed

explanation: Fear, stigma, and trying traditional remedies first are real barriers our patients face. As nurses, part of our job is compassionate, judgment-free education. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h3)

question: Which viral infection is a major risk factor for liver cancer?

options.A: Influenza A
options.B: Hepatitis B
options.C: Varicella Zoster
options.D: Rabies virus

explanation: Chronic Hepatitis B causes long-term inflammation and scarring in the liver, which can eventually lead to liver cancer. Vaccination is key! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h4)

question: Why is smoking tobacco such a major risk factor for many types of cancer?

options.A: It introduces living cancer cells into the lungs
options.B: It blocks all major blood vessels
options.C: It contains harmful chemicals that damage cellular DNA
options.D: It stops red blood cells from forming

explanation: Tobacco smoke has active chemical carcinogens that mess up the genetic code inside healthy cells, triggering abnormal growth. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h4)

question: During a Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA) screening for cervical pre-cancer, what liquid is applied to the cervix?

options.A: Iodine tincture
options.B: Vinegar
options.C: Hydrogen peroxide
options.D: Normal saline

explanation: Acetic acid is simply the active ingredient in vinegar! It makes abnormal cells temporarily turn white so the nurse can spot them easily. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of cancer screening programs in primary health care?

options.A: To find out the patient's family tree
options.B: To completely replace laboratory blood tests
options.C: To perform major cancer surgeries
options.D: To catch abnormalities before symptoms and spreading happen

explanation: Screening is all about catching issues early when treatment is easiest and most successful. Prevention is better than cure! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h5)

question: In the famous 'CAUTION' warning signs of cancer, what does the letter 'U' stand for?

options.A: Unexplained weight gain
options.B: Urinary tract infection
options.C: Unusual bleeding or discharge
options.D: Ulceration of the skin

explanation: Remember CAUTION! The 'U' reminds us to never ignore unexplained bleeding or discharge from any part of the body. Keep that in your nursing toolkit! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h6)

question: A patient has had a hoarse voice and a nagging cough for over three months that won't go away with antibiotics. Which cancer warning sign does this match?

options.A: Difficulty swallowing food
options.B: Obvious change in a mole
options.C: Change in bowel habits
options.D: Nagging cough or hoarseness

explanation: That's the 'N' in CAUTION: a nagging cough or hoarseness. When a symptom sticks around way too long, it's time for a deeper check-up! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h6)

question: How should pain medication be given for chronic cancer pain according to standard guidelines?

options.A: Only when the pain becomes unbearable
options.B: Only when the patient remembers to ask
options.C: On a regular schedule around the clock
options.D: Strictly as a single bedtime dose

explanation: Scheduled dosing keeps the pain under control smoothly, rather than waiting for it to spike and trying to chase it down. Smart nursing care! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h7)

question: Why do many advanced cancer patients experience severe weight loss and muscle wasting?

options.A: Permanent blockage of the large intestine only
options.B: A total loss of the brain's thirst center
options.C: Being forced to do too much heavy exercise
options.D: Metabolic changes caused by the tumor and treatments

explanation: Cancer changes how the body uses energy, leading to a condition called cachexia where muscle and fat break down fast. Nutritional support is so vital here. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h7)

question: What is the primary focus of palliative care?

options.A: To speed up the dying process
options.B: To replace hospital chemotherapy entirely
options.C: To improve quality of life and relieve suffering
options.D: To completely cure aggressive tumors

explanation: Palliative care is all about comfort, dignity, and making sure patients and their families feel supported when a cure isn't possible. Beautiful, compassionate nursing! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h8)

question: Why is community health education so crucial for fighting cancer in Nigeria?

options.A: It replaces the need for palliative nurses
options.B: It guarantees free surgeries at every health post
options.C: It helps clear up harmful myths and encourages early hospital visits
options.D: It completely stops genetic mutations from happening

explanation: When we educate our communities with love and facts, we break down fear and cultural barriers so people seek help early. You are going to make a great nurse! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T15#GNS214_U1_T15_h8)

question: What is the primary abnormal protein found in the red blood cells of a person with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Haemoglobin F
options.B: Haemoglobin C
options.C: Haemoglobin A
options.D: Haemoglobin S

explanation: The genetic mutation in sickle cell anaemia specifically leads to the production of abnormal haemoglobin S, which changes the shape of the red blood cells when it loses oxygen. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h1)

question: Why do red blood cells change into a sickle shape in this condition?

options.A: The bone marrow produces cells with too much iron and water inside them
options.B: Haemoglobin S molecules stick together to form rigid rods when they release oxygen
options.C: White blood cells attack and deform the healthy red blood cells
options.D: Excess sugar in the bloodstream causes the red blood cells to shrink and warp

explanation: When haemoglobin S delivers oxygen to body tissues, it clumps into stiff strands that distort the normal round cell into a crescent shape. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h1)

question: What genotype represents a person who carries the sickle cell trait without having the full disease?

options.A: SS
options.B: AA
options.C: SC
options.D: AS

explanation: Genotype AS means the individual has one normal gene and one mutated gene, making them a healthy carrier of the trait. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h2)

question: What must happen for a child to be born with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Only the mother needs to have the full sickle cell disease
options.B: The child must be exposed to severe malaria during infancy
options.C: Both parents must pass on a copy of the mutated sickle cell gene
options.D: Either parent must have genotype AS while the other has genotype AA

explanation: Because it is an autosomal recessive condition, a child needs two copies of the abnormal gene, requiring both parents to contribute a sickle gene. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h2)

question: What is the medical term for the yellowing of the skin and eyes caused by the rapid breakdown of red blood cells?

options.A: Cyanosis
options.B: Jaundice
options.C: Pallor
options.D: Erythema

explanation: Jaundice happens when red blood cells break down quickly, releasing excess bilirubin which the liver processes more slowly than it is produced. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h3)

question: Why are children with sickle cell anaemia at a much higher risk of severe bacterial infections?

options.A: Low dietary iron intake weakens the entire immune system from birth
options.B: The bone marrow stops producing white blood cells to make more sickled cells
options.C: Repeated blood vessel blockages eventually damage and destroy spleen function
options.D: Abnormal haemoglobin coats bacteria and prevents immune cells from seeing them

explanation: The spleen filters bacteria and helps fight infections, but repeated sickling clogs its vessels until it stops working entirely, a process called auto-splenectomy. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h3)

question: What is the most common trigger for a vaso-occlusive pain crisis in a patient with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Taking daily folic acid supplements
options.B: Dehydration or infection
options.C: Eating high-protein meals
options.D: Sleeping on a firm mattress

explanation: Dehydration thickens the blood and infections increase physical stress, both of which easily trigger blood cells to sickle and block vessels. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h4)

question: A patient with sickle cell anaemia is admitted in a painful vaso-occlusive crisis. Which immediate nursing intervention should be prioritized?

options.A: Preparing the patient for immediate surgical removal of the spleen
options.B: Restricting fluid intake to prevent fluid overload in the lungs
options.C: Administering prescribed pain medication and encouraging fluids
options.D: Encouraging heavy physical exercise to improve circulation

explanation: Managing pain and rehydrating the patient to thin the blood and restore circulation are the immediate priorities during an acute crisis. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h4)

question: Which laboratory test is considered the gold standard for confirming a diagnosis of sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Sickle solubility test
options.B: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
options.C: Haemoglobin electrophoresis
options.D: Full blood count

explanation: Haemoglobin electrophoresis separates the different types of haemoglobin proteins to provide a definitive diagnosis of the specific genotype. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h5)

question: What does an elevated reticulocyte count in a routine blood test usually indicate in a patient with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Iron supplements are building up to toxic levels in the blood
options.B: The patient is experiencing a sudden kidney infection
options.C: The spleen has successfully cleared all abnormal cells from circulation
options.D: The bone marrow is working hard to replace destroyed red blood cells

explanation: Reticulocytes are newly formed red blood cells. A high count shows the bone marrow is rushing to make new cells to make up for those lost to haemolysis. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h5)

question: Why is malaria prevention especially critical for individuals living with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Anti-malarial medications cure the underlying genetic mutation permanently
options.B: Malaria infection triggers severe red blood cell sickling and life-threatening crises
options.C: Malaria parasites feed directly on normal adult haemoglobin A exclusively
options.D: Fever from malaria permanently stops the bone marrow from making blood

explanation: Fever, inflammation, and red blood cell destruction caused by malaria are powerful triggers that induce widespread vessel blockage in sickle cell patients. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h6)

question: What is the main reason young children with sickle cell anaemia are given daily prophylactic penicillin?

options.A: To prevent severe bacterial infections due to reduced spleen function
options.B: To stop malaria parasites from entering the bloodstream during the rainy season
options.C: To stimulate the bone marrow to produce more flexible red blood cells
options.D: To reduce chronic joint pain caused by dactylitis in the fingers and toes

explanation: Because the spleen loses its ability to filter bacteria early in life, daily penicillin protects these children from dangerous encapsulated bacterial infections. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h6)

question: Which lifestyle advice is most important for a nurse to emphasize during patient education for sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Restrict fluid intake in the evening to prevent frequent nighttime urination
options.B: Maintain consistent daily hydration and avoid extreme temperature changes
options.C: Wear tight, supportive clothing to keep the peripheral blood vessels compressed
options.D: Engage in intense competitive sports to build strong cardiovascular endurance

explanation: Drinking plenty of water prevents the blood from thickening, and avoiding cold temperatures stops blood vessels from narrowing, both of which prevent crises. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h7)

question: A mother brings her young child with sickle cell anaemia to the clinic. Which statement by the mother shows she understands home care instructions?

options.A: We stopped the daily penicillin because our child has not been sick lately
options.B: We avoid letting our child eat any green vegetables containing folic acid
options.C: I only give pain medication when the swelling in the fingers becomes unbearable
options.D: I make sure my child drinks plenty of water every day, even when feeling well

explanation: Consistent daily hydration keeps red blood cells flowing smoothly and is a cornerstone of preventing painful vaso-occlusive episodes at home. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h7)

question: What is the term for the bone tissue death in the hip or shoulder caused by blocked blood supply in sickle cell patients?

options.A: Avascular necrosis
options.B: Osteomyelitis
options.C: Osteoporosis
options.D: Dactylitis

explanation: Avascular necrosis occurs when restricted blood flow deprives bone tissue of oxygen and nutrients, causing the bone to break down over time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h8)

question: Why is regular multi-disciplinary follow-up essential for adults living with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: To monitor and manage progressive long-term damage to major body organs
options.B: To perform routine blood transfusions that reverse the abnormal gene sequence
options.C: To prevent the patient from ever experiencing another painful crisis again
options.D: To ensure the patient takes daily antibiotics to cure the genetic mutation

explanation: Chronic organ damage to the kidneys, lungs, brain, and joints accumulates over years, requiring coordinated specialist care to catch and treat complications early. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h8)

question: What is the main goal of good nutrition in Primary Health Care (PHC)?

options.A: Replacing clinical treatments with herbal remedies
options.B: Preventing deficiency diseases and supporting optimal potential
options.C: Eliminating the need for agricultural market regulations
options.D: Reducing the cost of commercial food imports

explanation: You got this! In PHC, good nutrition is all about helping people stay healthy, avoiding illness, and reaching their full body and mind development. Keep it up! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T17#GNS214_U1_T17_h1)

question: Why must community nurses look beyond the clinic when dealing with poor nutrition?

options.A: Because nutrition problems only exist inside large hospital wards
options.B: Because hospital management forbids nurses from talking about food
options.C: Because clinical medications can cure malnutrition completely on their own
options.D: Because root causes like poverty and food disruption require community-based action

explanation: Spot on! Nutritional challenges are often tied to bigger social and economic issues. Giving medicine alone isn't enough—we need community action and education too. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T17#GNS214_U1_T17_h1)

question: What do we call the main nutrients that give the body bulk energy and building blocks?

options.A: Antioxidants
options.B: Electrolytes
options.C: Micronutrients
options.D: Macronutrients

explanation: Great job! Macronutrients include carbs, proteins, and fats. They are the big players that supply your daily energy and physical structure. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T17#GNS214_U1_T17_h2)

question: What does 'hidden hunger' mean in community nutrition?

options.A: Eating enough calories from starchy foods while lacking vital micronutrients
options.B: A sudden shortage of food caused by severe drought conditions
options.C: A psychological condition where patients refuse to eat despite starving
options.D: The physical sensation of hunger felt late at night

explanation: Exactly! Hidden hunger happens when someone gets enough food to fill their stomach (like heavy swallows of starch), but their diet misses the key vitamins and minerals they really need. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T17#GNS214_U1_T17_h2)

question: What is the main use of MUAC tape during community health outreaches?

options.A: To quickly screen for acute malnutrition using a simple tape
options.B: To determine the daily caloric intake of a household
options.C: To test blood sugar levels for diabetes screening
options.D: To calculate the exact body mass index of adult men

explanation: Well done! Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) uses color-coded tapes to quickly check if infants or young children are suffering from sudden, severe malnutrition. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T17#GNS214_U1_T17_h3)

question: A nurse notices more children losing weight in the months right before the new harvest. What activity helped spot this trend?

options.A: Individual genetic sequencing
options.B: Surgical theater auditing
options.C: Hospital pharmacy inventory check
options.D: Community nutritional status monitoring

explanation: Spot on! Tracking how nutrition changes across different seasons helps nurses spot recurring health issues in the whole community before they get out of hand. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T17#GNS214_U1_T17_h3)

question: What is a big plus of having homestead gardens in rural areas?

options.A: Eliminating the need for any community health education
options.B: Generating large profits on international export markets
options.C: Providing immediate access to fresh vegetables and fruits
options.D: Replacing local health clinics with herbal gardens

explanation: You got it! Homestead gardens mean families can just walk to their backyard to grab fresh, nutritious greens without needing extra cash or long travel. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T17#GNS214_U1_T17_h4)

question: Why is proper post-harvest management important for food security?

options.A: It increases the chemical fertilizer content in staple grains
options.B: It removes the need for farmers to rotate their crops
options.C: It forces farmers to sell all their crops immediately after harvesting
options.D: It prevents food loss from pests and spoilage during lean periods

explanation: Correct! Storing and preserving food properly keeps it safe from pests so families have something to eat even when crops are scarce. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T17#GNS214_U1_T17_h4)

question: What is the main focus of Behavioral Change Communication (BCC) in nutrition?

options.A: Addressing cultural habits and beliefs influencing food choices
options.B: Importing expensive nutritional supplements from abroad
options.C: Enforcing strict legal penalties for poor dietary habits
options.D: Conducting laboratory tests on food chemical safety

explanation: That's right! BCC looks past simple facts to understand the cultural and social reasons behind how people choose and prepare their meals. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T17#GNS214_U1_T17_h5)

question: Why do nurses promote local foods during cooking demos instead of imported ones?

options.A: Local health policies legally forbid the use of foreign recipes
options.B: Local ingredients are usually more affordable and accessible to the community
options.C: Imported foods cause immediate illness in all age groups
options.D: Imported foods are always completely devoid of any nutritional value

explanation: Spot on! Good nutrition teaching has to be practical. Using foods that families can easily buy or grow nearby ensures the habit sticks. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T17#GNS214_U1_T17_h5)

question: Which deficiency condition is marked by severe muscle wasting and very little body fat?

options.A: Night blindness
options.B: Goiter
options.C: Kwashiorkor
options.D: Marasmus

explanation: You're doing great! Marasmus is a severe lack of energy and protein where a child looks extremely thin and wasted away because of absent body fat. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T17#GNS214_U1_T17_h6)

question: What is the primary public health way to prevent iodine deficiency in a population?

options.A: Providing Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food packets
options.B: Distributing high-dose vitamin A capsules
options.C: Promoting the universal use of iodized salt
options.D: Administering iron-folate tablets to infants

explanation: Correct! Iodized salt is the simplest, most effective way to reach everyone and stop conditions like goiter from developing. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T17#GNS214_U1_T17_h6)

question: What does intersectoral collaboration mean when working on food security?

options.A: Working together across different fields like agriculture, health, and education
options.B: Relying solely on nursing staff to manage agricultural projects
options.C: Merging all hospitals into a single centralized government agency
options.D: Importing food supplies exclusively from neighboring countries

explanation: Spot on! Because food security involves farming, schooling, and healthcare, different ministries and sectors must join hands to fix it. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T17#GNS214_U1_T17_h7)

question: Why is the agricultural sector so important when health workers try to improve nutrition?

options.A: Because farming practices have no impact on community health outcomes
options.B: Because farmers are legally required to diagnose nutritional deficiencies
options.C: Because agricultural workers manage all rural health clinics
options.D: Because agriculture determines how much and what types of food are produced

explanation: Brilliant! Farming dictates what food is available and how varied the food supply is, making agriculture the very foundation of good nutrition. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T17#GNS214_U1_T17_h7)

question: Why do governments create food and nutrition policies?

options.A: To completely ban bringing any foreign food into the country
options.B: To control the exact daily price of goods in local markets
options.C: To manage employment records for all farm workers
options.D: To connect what farmers grow directly with what communities need to stay healthy

explanation: Food policies help make sure that farming output meets the actual nutritional health needs of the population. Great job thinking about the big picture! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h1)

question: As a nurse, why is it helpful to understand national food policies?

options.A: Clinical nutritional counseling fails if patients cannot access or afford recommended foods
options.B: Nurses decide the specific types of seeds farmers must plant
options.C: Nurses are legally required to inspect commercial farms for safety
options.D: Clinical staff must directly distribute farming money to local villages

explanation: When you give dietary advice to a patient, you have to know what food is actually available and affordable in their community! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h1)

question: What does 'food security' mean for a population?

options.A: Storing a ten-year supply of grains in underground bunkers
options.B: Having military protection around every food warehouse
options.C: Constant physical, social, and economic access to safe and enough food
options.D: Producing every single food item inside the country's borders

explanation: Food security simply means everyone has reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food to live a healthy life. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h2)

question: How do government irrigation projects help boost farming?

options.A: By reducing total dependence on seasonal rainfall for farming
options.B: By lowering the market price of chemical fertilizers
options.C: By giving formal land certificates to rural farmers
options.D: By providing cash loans to farmer groups

explanation: Irrigation gives crops water even during dry seasons, which means farmers can grow food all year round. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h2)

question: What is the main job of cold chain logistics in the food supply chain?

options.A: To keep transport vehicles cool for drivers on long trips
options.B: To freeze-dry grains for underground storage
options.C: To prevent the rapid spoilage of perishable items like milk and meat
options.D: To kill weed seeds in harvested crops before milling

explanation: Cold chain systems use refrigeration to keep perishable foods fresh and safe all the way from the farm to your plate. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h3)

question: Why do bad rural feeder roads hurt national food security?

options.A: They force the government to import all staple foods
options.B: They delay transport, causing high spoilage rates and high food prices in cities
options.C: They stop farmers from getting chemical fertilizers and seeds
options.D: They make it illegal for farmers to sell crops across state lines

explanation: When roads are poor, food gets stuck or damaged on the way, leading to waste and higher prices for people in the city. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h3)

question: What is a major cause of post-harvest food loss in farming communities?

options.A: Pest infestations and poor drying techniques
options.B: Strict international export inspections
options.C: Excessive government taxes on farm tools
options.D: Mandatory crop rotation laws from local councils

explanation: Bad storage, pests, and moisture can destroy a huge portion of crops right after harvest before they ever make it to market. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h4)

question: Why is making sure grains are properly dried before storage a vital health measure?

options.A: It prevents the growth of molds that produce dangerous aflatoxins
options.B: It stops insects from eating metal storage silos
options.C: It guarantees the seeds will sprout next season
options.D: It makes the grain weigh less during transport

explanation: Wet grain grows mold easily, and that mold makes toxins called aflatoxins that can seriously harm the liver when eaten. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT something food safety regulations normally check for?

options.A: Physical objects like metal shards or stones
options.B: Dangerous levels of chemical pesticide residues
options.C: Political views of the food manufacturing company owners
options.D: Harmful germs causing foodborne illnesses

explanation: Food safety is strictly about biological, chemical, and physical hazards—not who owns the company or what they believe! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h5)

question: Why do food safety officers frequently inspect local open-air markets and street food vendors?

options.A: These vendors feed a huge portion of the urban working-class population
options.B: Street vendors have more money to pay official fines
options.C: Open markets never have contamination problems
options.D: Large supermarkets are legally exempt from all safety checks

explanation: Since millions of people buy from local markets and street vendors every day, keeping those foods safe is crucial for public health. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h5)

question: What is a key everyday duty for health workers when it comes to food policy?

options.A: Writing the national budget for farm machinery
options.B: Designing state highways for food transport trucks
options.C: Conducting infant growth monitoring to spot early signs of malnutrition
options.D: Issuing business licenses to big food factories

explanation: As health workers, we put policy into action right at the clinic by checking children's growth and catching malnutrition early. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h6)

question: A community nurse notices a sudden outbreak of severe diarrhea in one neighborhood. What is the best immediate step?

options.A: Tell all residents to stop eating food completely for a week
options.B: Report the outbreak to local authorities and investigate contaminated food sources
options.C: Request farming grants for local grain producers
options.D: Order heavy machinery to dig up the local market

explanation: Frontline health workers must quickly report suspected outbreaks and trace the source to stop others from getting sick. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h6)

question: What is a major challenge that stops agricultural and food policies from succeeding?

options.A: Having too many trained nurses working as policy makers
options.B: Inadequate funding and a lack of follow-through when governments change
options.C: People refusing to eat locally grown foods
options.D: Having too much cold storage in every single village

explanation: Frequent political shifts and poor funding often leave great agricultural policies unfinished. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h7)

question: Why do health, agriculture, and environment ministries need to work together on food policies?

options.A: It ensures the health ministry controls the whole budget
options.B: It is just a rule required by international banks
options.C: Food production, safety, and nutrition cut across all of these sectors
options.D: It stops farm workers from practicing nursing in clinics

explanation: Solving big food challenges takes teamwork between farming experts, environmentalists, and healthcare professionals! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h7)

question: What is the main goal of doing a nutritional check on a patient in primary health care?

options.A: To evaluate nutritional status and spot early signs of health issues
options.B: To calculate the exact household income of a patient
options.C: To prescribe expensive vitamin supplements for every patient
options.D: To diagnose rare genetic disorders affecting body weight

explanation: Spotting poor nutrition early helps you step in with advice before the patient gets seriously ill. You've got this! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h1)

question: Why is it helpful for a nurse to assess the nutrition of an entire family rather than just one person?

options.A: Family members always have identical nutritional requirements
options.B: Individual assessments are legally prohibited in community clinics
options.C: Hospital policies require whole-family admission for dietary advice
options.D: Families usually share similar eating habits and money challenges

explanation: Looking at the whole family helps you see the big picture—like what kind of food is cooked at home and what challenges everyone faces together. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h1)

question: Which body measurement is most commonly used in the community to quickly screen young children for severe malnutrition?

options.A: Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC)
options.B: Total body surface area
options.C: Waist-to-hip ratio
options.D: Head circumference

explanation: The MUAC tape is a nurse's best friend during community outreaches—it's fast, easy, and great for checking young children on the spot! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h2)

question: A community nurse needs a quick, easy way to check for sudden fluid loss or weight gain in an adult. What should they use?

options.A: A weighing scale
options.B: A blood pressure cuff
options.C: A skinfold caliper
options.D: A sterile measuring tape

explanation: Never underestimate the power of a simple scale! Regular weighing is the easiest way to catch sudden fluid shifts or weight changes. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h2)

question: Which parts of the body usually show signs of vitamin or nutrient shortages first?

options.A: Parts with fast-growing cells like skin, hair, and nails
options.B: Major blood vessels and heart valves
options.C: Hard tissues like bones and deep skeletal muscles
options.D: Internal organs like the liver and kidneys

explanation: Because skin, hair, and nails replace their cells so quickly, they show signs of trouble way before deeper tissues do. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h3)

question: Why shouldn't a nurse rely only on visual physical checks when diagnosing malnutrition?

options.A: Clinical signs only appear after the patient is completely cured
options.B: Laboratory tests are illegal to perform in primary health clinics
options.C: Different nutrient shortages can cause very similar physical signs
options.D: Patients usually hide their physical symptoms from healthcare workers

explanation: Many deficiencies look alike on the outside. That's why we always back up our physical exams with diet histories and lab tests! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h3)

question: What does 'family food security' mean?

options.A: Having a locked storage room to protect food from insects
options.B: Having reliable access to enough safe, healthy food for everyone
options.C: Eating meals at the exact same time every single day
options.D: Growing all the family food on a private farm without buying anything

explanation: Food security simply means the household consistently has enough safe and nutritious food to live a healthy, active life. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h4)

question: What is the main drawback of using a 24-hour food recall to check what a patient eats?

options.A: It requires expensive laboratory equipment to calculate
options.B: Patients may forget or misreport what they actually ate
options.C: It only measures physical height rather than food
options.D: It takes over a week to complete a single interview

explanation: Memory can be tricky! Clients might easily forget that little afternoon snack or misjudge the size of their food portions. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h4)

question: Which common lab test is used to screen patients for anemia?

options.A: Liver function enzymes
options.B: Serum lipid profile
options.C: Fast blood glucose
options.D: Hemoglobin and hematocrit

explanation: Checking hemoglobin and hematocrit tells us how well the blood carries oxygen, making it the go-to test for anemia. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h5)

question: Why can a sudden infection mess up the results of a patient's blood protein test?

options.A: Infections trigger body changes that alter protein levels regardless of diet
options.B: Lab technicians are not allowed to run protein tests during an illness
options.C: Infections destroy all blood drawing needles in the clinic
options.D: Infection automatically cures any existing vitamin deficiency

explanation: Inflammation from an infection can drive blood protein levels down, which might trick you into thinking the patient is starving when they actually have an infection. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h5)

question: Why are infants and young children considered a nutritionally vulnerable group?

options.A: Their rapid growth and development require lots of nutrients
options.B: Their bodies do not require protein during early childhood
options.C: They possess fully developed immune systems that reject food
options.D: They refuse to eat any form of solid food until age five

explanation: Kids grow so fast! If their diet falls short even a little bit, it can quickly lead to poor growth or malnutrition. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h6)

question: An elderly patient reports poor appetite, trouble chewing, and losing weight without trying. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: A sudden increase in daily physical growth velocity
options.B: An allergic reaction to drinking clean tap water
options.C: An excessive desire to run marathon races every week
options.D: Age-related dental challenges and a reduced appetite

explanation: As people get older, dental issues, changes in taste, and lower appetite often make eating tougher, putting them at risk of poor nutrition. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h6)

question: What should be a nurse's main focus when giving diet advice to a low-income family?

options.A: Advising them to eat only once every two days
options.B: Recommending affordable, locally available foods
options.C: Telling them to stop eating traditional family meals
options.D: Insisting they purchase expensive imported vitamins

explanation: Good nutrition advice has to be practical. Always recommend foods that the family can easily find and afford in their local market. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h7)

question: Why should community nutrition counseling respect local food traditions?

options.A: Families are much more likely to follow advice that fits their culture
options.B: Traditional recipes always contain zero nutritional value
options.C: Cultural habits prevent any form of weight gain
options.D: Nurses are legally forbidden from discussing local foods

explanation: When you work with a family's cultural food habits instead of fighting them, they are way more likely to stick with your healthy changes! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of IEC in primary health care?

options.A: To enforce strict government penalties for poor hygiene
options.B: To bridge the gap between health knowledge and community practice
options.C: To generate revenue for local health clinics
options.D: To replace clinical treatments with home remedies

explanation: IEC translates complex medical facts into practical actions that people can use daily. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T2#GNS214_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why is IEC considered a preventive tool in Nigerian health care?

options.A: It guarantees immunity against all known tropical diseases
options.B: It replaces the need for doctors in primary health centers
options.C: It provides free medications to every household in the village
options.D: It stops diseases before they start by promoting healthy behaviors

explanation: Educating the public on hygiene and prevention reduces the burden of diseases before clinical intervention is needed. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T2#GNS214_U1_T2_h1)

question: A common prevailing health problem requiring targeted IEC in many Nigerian communities is:

options.A: Industrial chemical poisoning
options.B: Rare genetic metabolic disorders
options.C: Malaria and preventable childhood illnesses
options.D: Chronic altitude sickness

explanation: Malaria and vaccine-preventable diseases are major public health priorities across Nigerian communities. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T2#GNS214_U1_T2_h2)

question: A community health nurse wants to know the most urgent health issue in a rural settlement. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Report the village leaders to the state ministry
options.B: Distribute mosquito nets immediately without asking questions
options.C: Conduct a needs assessment using interviews and surveys
options.D: Build a new primary health care center

explanation: Gathering baseline data ensures that health campaigns address the actual challenges faced by the residents. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T2#GNS214_U1_T2_h2)

question: What makes Behavior Change Communication different from basic information sharing?

options.A: It relies exclusively on written pamphlets and textbooks
options.B: It addresses social and cultural factors influencing daily habits
options.C: It is handled only by medical doctors in tertiary hospitals
options.D: It focuses solely on distributing medical equipment

explanation: BCC goes beyond giving facts to actively target the underlying drivers of human behavior. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T2#GNS214_U1_T2_h3)

question: Why is two-way communication essential during health education sessions?

options.A: It ensures that meetings finish much faster
options.B: It stops people from disagreeing with health policies
options.C: It prevents nurses from speaking during community meetings
options.D: It allows community members to ask questions and share concerns

explanation: Dialogue builds trust and clears up misunderstandings that a one-way lecture might leave unaddressed. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T2#GNS214_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which medium is most effective for reaching remote rural settlements without steady electricity?

options.A: National television broadcasts
options.B: Social media banner ads
options.C: English-language medical journals
options.D: Town criers and drama groups

explanation: Traditional channels like town criers and drama groups do not rely on electricity and fit local traditions. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T2#GNS214_U1_T2_h4)

question: A nurse wants to reinforce instructions about infant immunization given during a clinic visit. Which material is best to give the mother to take home?

options.A: A radio set with extra batteries
options.B: A simple illustrated handbill or immunization card
options.C: A detailed textbook on immunology
options.D: A video cassette of a surgical operation

explanation: Simple print materials serve as a handy reminder of dates and home-care instructions after the visit. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T2#GNS214_U1_T2_h4)

question: Who should be engaged early to ensure high community acceptance of a health program?

options.A: Foreign tourists visiting the local market
options.B: Federal legislators in the national capital
options.C: Local stakeholders like traditional and religious leaders
options.D: International pharmaceutical manufacturing companies

explanation: Community leaders hold immense influence and can encourage their people to participate in health programs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T2#GNS214_U1_T2_h5)

question: What is the main benefit of community mobilization in public health interventions?

options.A: It forces residents to comply without asking questions
options.B: It removes the need for professional nurses in rural clinics
options.C: It ensures the government stops funding local hospitals
options.D: It turns community members into active partners in their own health

explanation: Mobilization fosters ownership, ensuring the community sustains health practices long after external support ends. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T2#GNS214_U1_T2_h5)

question: What is the difference between monitoring and evaluation in an IEC campaign?

options.A: Monitoring is illegal, while evaluation is mandatory
options.B: Monitoring focuses on finances, while evaluation focuses on buildings
options.C: Monitoring is done by villagers, while evaluation is done by politicians
options.D: Monitoring tracks ongoing activities, while evaluation measures final impact

explanation: Monitoring occurs during implementation to guide daily actions, whereas evaluation reviews the ultimate results. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T2#GNS214_U1_T2_h6)

question: Why is pre-testing IEC materials before a community campaign important?

options.A: It reduces the total cost of printing by half
options.B: It ensures the materials meet international export standards
options.C: It allows the nurse to copyright the health messages
options.D: It helps identify and fix confusing illustrations or cultural misunderstandings

explanation: Pre-testing ensures that the target audience easily understands the message without misinterpretation. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T2#GNS214_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of nutrition counselling in primary health care?

options.A: Guiding food choices to promote health and prevent disease
options.B: Prescribing expensive nutritional supplements for every patient
options.C: Enforcing strict hospital dietary restrictions on communities
options.D: Diagnosing rare metabolic disorders in a laboratory setting

explanation: Nutrition counselling focuses on helping clients make healthy food choices to prevent illness and support overall wellness in primary care. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h1)

question: Why is effective nutrition counselling more than just handing a patient a printed diet sheet?

options.A: It requires understanding the patient's daily life and financial limits.
options.B: Patients in rural communities usually cannot read printed materials.
options.C: Doctors are the only ones legally allowed to explain diet sheets.
options.D: Printed sheets are too expensive to produce in local clinics.

explanation: Real dietary guidance must fit a patient's actual living conditions, budget, and access to local food markets rather than being a generic list. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h1)

question: What physical measurement is commonly used in community settings to quickly screen young children for acute malnutrition?

options.A: Total body water volume
options.B: Resting metabolic rate
options.C: Mid-upper arm circumference
options.D: Sitting height ratio

explanation: Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is a quick, reliable screening tool used by nurses in the field to check for wasting in children. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h2)

question: A nurse wants to know a patient's actual food intake over the past day. Which assessment method is best suited for this?

options.A: A 24-hour dietary recall
options.B: An inpatient surgical biopsy
options.C: A two-week physical exercise log
options.D: A complete genetic blood screening

explanation: The 24-hour dietary recall asks the patient to list all foods and drinks consumed during the previous day to estimate nutrient intake. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h2)

question: Which group is most at risk for protein-energy malnutrition during the transition to family foods?

options.A: Healthy young adult athletes
options.B: Middle-aged male farmers
options.C: Infants and young children
options.D: Retired elderly office workers

explanation: Young children transitioning from breast milk or formula to family foods are at high risk if their new diet lacks sufficient nutrients. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h3)

question: Why do pregnant women have a significantly higher nutritional requirement for specific minerals like iron?

options.A: To support expanding blood volume and fetal growth
options.B: To completely prevent gestational diabetes mellitus
options.C: To replace electrolytes lost through morning sickness
options.D: To cure pre-existing chronic bone infections

explanation: Pregnancy causes a major increase in blood volume and requires extra nutrients to support the developing fetus and placenta. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h3)

question: What communication style works best to encourage a patient to adopt healthier eating habits?

options.A: A silent demonstration with no words
options.B: A strict and formal medical lecture
options.C: A rapid list of commands to follow
options.D: A collaborative and supportive dialogue

explanation: Working together through supportive conversation helps patients feel empowered rather than judged or forced. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h4)

question: Why are open-ended questions preferred over closed questions when taking a dietary history?

options.A: They encourage the patient to share more details about their actual habits.
options.B: They allow the nurse to finish the consultation without speaking.
options.C: They take much less time to complete during busy clinic shifts.
options.D: They legally protect the hospital from documentation errors.

explanation: Open-ended questions prevent patients from giving simple yes or no answers, revealing more accurate information about their true diet. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h4)

question: How should a nurse handle a cultural food taboo that limits a pregnant woman's protein intake?

options.A: Ignore the food taboo completely and focus only on vitamin supplements
options.B: Provide respectful education while suggesting nutritious local alternatives
options.C: Mock the cultural belief to force the patient into immediate compliance
options.D: Report the family to local community authorities for traditional practices

explanation: Respectful dialogue and culturally sensitive education work best to address harmful myths without alienating the patient or community. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h5)

question: A mother on a tight budget needs affordable protein sources for her growing toddlers. Which local foods should the nurse recommend?

options.A: Beans, groundnuts, and local fish
options.B: Processed energy bars from abroad
options.C: Expensive dietary protein powders
options.D: Imported canned salmon and caviar

explanation: Locally available plant and animal proteins like beans, groundnuts, and fish are cost-effective and culturally appropriate options. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of scheduling follow-up nutrition appointments with a patient?

options.A: To test the patient's memory on dietary terminology
options.B: To monitor progress and adjust meal plans as needed
options.C: To collect extra administrative fees for the clinic
options.D: To penalize the patient for failing to gain weight

explanation: Follow-ups give nurses a chance to see what is working, troubleshoot new barriers, and keep the patient motivated. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h6)

question: Why is it important for a nurse to identify financial or social barriers before giving a diet plan?

options.A: To comply with federal tax reporting laws for healthcare workers
options.B: To decide whether the patient qualifies for free inpatient medical care
options.C: To prove that the nurse understands the local economic situation
options.D: To ensure the recommended meal plan is realistic and affordable for the family

explanation: Understanding financial limits prevents the nurse from prescribing foods the patient cannot afford or store, ensuring better compliance. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h6)

question: What is the main goal of food safety in primary health care?

options.A: Disease prevention and health promotion
options.B: Regulating international food trade
options.C: Managing surgical theatre sterility
options.D: Treating advanced chronic illnesses

explanation: You've got this! Food safety at the primary health care level is all about stopping foodborne illnesses before they start and helping our communities stay healthy and strong. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T21#GNS214_U1_T21_h1)

question: Why is food safety such a big priority for community health nurses?

options.A: It directly reduces preventable gastrointestinal infections
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for community health clinics
options.C: It is the only way to treat chronic medical conditions
options.D: It stops all forms of malnutrition instantly

explanation: Spot on! When we teach and practice good food safety, we cut down massively on those painful, preventable stomach infections that bring patients into our clinics. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T21#GNS214_U1_T21_h1)

question: Why do we always keep raw meat separate from ready-to-eat foods?

options.A: To speed up the cooking process
options.B: To improve the overall taste of the meal
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of cooking
options.D: To prevent cross-contamination of harmful bacteria

explanation: Think of it like keeping bad company away from good! Separating raw meat stops dangerous germs from jumping onto foods that won't be cooked again before eating. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T21#GNS214_U1_T21_h2)

question: How does putting perishable food in the fridge right away help protect health?

options.A: It turns raw ingredients into ready-to-eat meals
options.B: It completely kills all existing viruses in meat
options.C: It slows down bacterial multiplication in perishable foods
options.D: It removes chemical toxins from spoiled vegetables

explanation: Brilliant! Fridges don't kill bacteria, but the cold temperature acts like a brake, slowing down how fast those tiny germs can grow and multiply. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T21#GNS214_U1_T21_h2)

question: Which specific bacterium causes cholera?

options.A: Staphylococcus aureus
options.B: Salmonella typhi
options.C: Vibrio cholerae
options.D: Escherichia coli

explanation: Great recall! Cholera is caused by *Vibrio cholerae*, a bacterium that loves to hitch a ride in contaminated water and food supplies. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T21#GNS214_U1_T21_h3)

question: A patient comes to your clinic with severe watery diarrhea and sudden, rapid dehydration after eating food from a roadside vendor. What condition should you suspect first?

options.A: Cholera
options.B: Asthma exacerbation
options.C: Chronic hypertension
options.D: Iron deficiency anemia

explanation: You nailed it. Sudden, severe watery diarrhea and rapid dehydration after eating questionable food are classic red flags for cholera. Quick fluid replacement is key here! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T21#GNS214_U1_T21_h3)

question: When washing hands as a food handler, how long should you scrub with soap and water?

options.A: At least twenty seconds
options.B: Until they feel completely dry
options.C: Exactly five seconds
options.D: About two minutes

explanation: Good hygiene is our best shield! Scrubbing with soap for at least twenty seconds gives the soap enough time to lift away and destroy harmful germs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T21#GNS214_U1_T21_h4)

question: Why is it unsafe to leave frozen meat sitting on a warm kitchen counter to thaw?

options.A: It causes the meat to lose all of its nutritional value
options.B: It freezes the center of the meat even harder
options.C: Surface bacteria multiply rapidly as the outer layers warm up
options.D: It turns the meat into a poisonous chemical substance

explanation: Makes total sense, right? As the outer layers warm up to room temperature, they enter the 'danger zone' where bacteria throw a party and multiply fast. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T21#GNS214_U1_T21_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a safe way to treat drinking water?

options.A: Adding appropriate chlorine treatment
options.B: Boiling it thoroughly
options.C: Storing it uncovered in a warm, dusty corner
options.D: Using a certified water filtration system

explanation: Exactly! Leaving clean water uncovered is an open invitation for dust, flies, and germs to sneak right back in and contaminate it. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T21#GNS214_U1_T21_h5)

question: How do open refuse dumps contribute to foodborne illnesses in a community?

options.A: They cause the air temperature in the kitchen to rise too high
options.B: They attract pests like flies and rodents that transfer pathogens to food
options.C: They increase the mineral content of nearby groundwater supplies
options.D: They remove all helpful bacteria from the local environment

explanation: You got it! Pests love open garbage; flies and rats feed on the dirt and then march right over uncovers food, leaving dangerous germs behind. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T21#GNS214_U1_T21_h5)

question: Why is it smart for community health nurses to work with local market leaders when promoting food hygiene?

options.A: It stops people from selling food altogether
options.B: It guarantees that the local market will receive government funding
options.C: It helps ensure the hygiene messages are accepted and practiced by vendors
options.D: It allows the nurse to avoid visiting the market stalls personally

explanation: Teamwork makes the dream work! Market leaders are respected, so getting them on board makes food vendors much more willing to listen and adopt safe habits. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T21#GNS214_U1_T21_h6)

question: You notice local food vendors leaving cooked rice uncovered in an open market stall. What is the best first step to take?

options.A: Provide practical education on food protection and cover methods
options.B: Close down all food businesses in the region permanently
options.C: Imprison the vendors without warning or explanation
options.D: Ignore the practice since it is a traditional custom

explanation: Fantastic nursing judgment! As public health nurses, our first superpower is education. Always teach and guide before jumping to harsh punishments. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T21#GNS214_U1_T21_h6)

question: What is the main goal of diet therapy in patient care?

options.A: Modifying regular food intake to meet specific health needs
options.B: Reducing hospital kitchen operational costs
options.C: Ensuring every patient eats the exact same meal
options.D: Replacing all forms of medical drug treatment

explanation: You've got this! Diet therapy is simply tailoring a patient's nutrition to help them heal, manage an illness, or balance their body's needs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T22#GNS214_U1_T22_h1)

question: Why is diet therapy such an important part of your daily nursing duties?

options.A: Nurses must personally cook all meals served in the hospital ward
options.B: Nurses are responsible for monitoring patient tolerance and supporting the prescribed nutrition plan
options.C: Dietary plans replace the need for physical assessments
options.D: Doctors never check what patients are eating

explanation: Since you spend the most time with patients, you are in the best position to see if they are enjoying their food and how well their body is handling it! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T22#GNS214_U1_T22_h1)

question: When you measure a patient's mid-upper arm circumference and body mass index, what kind of assessment are you doing?

options.A: Environmental factors
options.B: Biochemical data
options.C: Clinical signs
options.D: Anthropometric measurements

explanation: Don't let the big word scare you! 'Anthropometric' just means measuring physical body sizes like height, weight, and arm circumference to check nutrition. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T22#GNS214_U1_T22_h2)

question: You check a patient's lab results, like serum albumin and electrolytes. What type of nutritional data is this?

options.A: Environmental data
options.B: Anthropometric data
options.C: Dietary history
options.D: Biochemical data

explanation: Spot on! Lab tests and blood markers give you biochemical data, showing what is happening inside the patient's body chemically. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T22#GNS214_U1_T22_h2)

question: A patient just had jaw surgery and cannot chew solid foods. Which diet type is best for them?

options.A: High sodium diet
options.B: Standard regular diet
options.C: High residue diet
options.D: Soft or mechanical diet

explanation: Easy choice! Soft and mechanical diets change the texture of food so it's super easy to chew and swallow when the mouth or jaw needs a break. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T22#GNS214_U1_T22_h3)

question: What is a major risk if a recovering patient stays on a clear liquid diet for too long?

options.A: It triggers sudden weight gain from excess fats
options.B: It causes severe high blood pressure
options.C: It permanently ruins the patient's sense of taste
options.D: It can lead to hospital-derived malnutrition due to very low calorie and nutrient content

explanation: Clear liquids are great at first, but they don't have enough energy and nutrients. Keeping patients on them too long starves their healing body! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T22#GNS214_U1_T22_h3)

question: What is the main dietary focus when caring for a patient with high blood pressure (hypertension)?

options.A: Sodium restriction
options.B: Zero fluid consumption
options.C: High protein loading
options.D: Unlimited sugar intake

explanation: You know this! Cutting down on salt (sodium) helps reduce fluid retention and lowers pressure inside the blood vessels. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T22#GNS214_U1_T22_h4)

question: A patient with type 2 diabetes asks why they need to eat more fiber. How should you explain it?

options.A: Fiber slows down digestion, which helps prevent sharp blood sugar spikes after meals
options.B: Fiber increases blood sugar levels rapidly for quick energy
options.C: Fiber completely cures diabetes within a few days of eating it
options.D: Fiber replaces the need to ever take diabetes medication again

explanation: Great nursing communication! Fiber slows down how fast sugar enters the blood, keeping those glucose levels nice and steady after eating. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T22#GNS214_U1_T22_h4)

question: In community health nursing, what are Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Foods (RUTF) mainly used for?

options.A: Replacing clean drinking water supplies
options.B: Treating high blood pressure in adults
options.C: Treating severe acute malnutrition safely at home
options.D: Preserving fresh vegetables without refrigeration

explanation: RUTFs are nutrient-packed pastes that save lives by helping severely malnourished children recover right at home without needing a hospital bed. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T22#GNS214_U1_T22_h5)

question: Why do primary health care nurses encourage families to use local foods like beans and groundnuts for children?

options.A: They contain zero calories and prevent childhood obesity
options.B: They provide affordable, accessible plant proteins and nutrients for growing children
options.C: They completely cure infectious diseases like malaria
options.D: They are the only foods that do not require cooking

explanation: Using cheap, locally available foods makes good nutrition practical and sustainable for everyday families in our communities. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T22#GNS214_U1_T22_h5)

question: Why is it so helpful to involve family members when giving diet counseling to a patient?

options.A: It prevents the patient from ever eating outside the home
options.B: Family members pay all the hospital medical bills
options.C: Family members usually prepare the household meals and manage food purchases
options.D: Family members are legally required to taste all hospital food first

explanation: Since family members are usually the ones cooking at home, bringing them into the conversation ensures the new diet is actually doable for the household! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T22#GNS214_U1_T22_h6)

question: A patient complains that their prescribed diet cuts out all their favorite cultural dishes and feels impossible. What is your best response?

options.A: Tell the patient they have no choice and must strictly obey the prescription
options.B: Work with the patient to find healthy substitutes and modify their favorite cultural meals
options.C: Ignore the complaint since food preferences do not affect health outcomes
options.D: Advise the patient to stop eating entirely until they adjust to the new menu

explanation: That's patient-centered care! Respecting their culture and tweaking their favorite meals makes it much more likely they will stick to the plan. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T22#GNS214_U1_T22_h6)

question: How can you tell over time if a patient's diet therapy is working successfully?

options.A: Weight trends and laboratory values
options.B: The brand of cutlery used for meals
options.C: The exact time the hospital kitchen opens
options.D: The color of the hospital room walls

explanation: Checking changes in body weight and lab results gives you clear, undeniable proof of how well the therapeutic diet is working. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T22#GNS214_U1_T22_h7)

question: What should you suspect first if a patient's lab results don't improve even though they claim to follow their diet?

options.A: The dietary plan, adherence, or overall treatment approach needs re-evaluation
options.B: The patient must be hiding food inside their mattress
options.C: The patient has been cured of the disease completely
options.D: Laboratory tests are never accurate in clinical practice

explanation: When numbers don't budge, it's a cue for the healthcare team to pause, check if the diet is truly working, and make adjustments together. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T22#GNS214_U1_T22_h7)

question: Which insect spreads the malaria parasite to humans?

options.A: Housefly
options.B: Female Anopheles mosquito
options.C: Tsetse fly
options.D: Male Culex mosquito

explanation: Spot on! Malaria is transmitted specifically when an infected female Anopheles mosquito bites looking for a blood meal. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why do pregnant women and young children get severe malaria so easily in Nigeria?

options.A: Their immune defenses are either developing or temporarily lowered
options.B: They have a naturally higher body temperature that attracts vectors
options.C: They spend more time outdoors during peak sunlight hours
options.D: Their diets lack the specific nutrients required to fight protozoa

explanation: You got it! Little ones are still building their immune defenses, and pregnancy naturally lowers a woman's immune response for a bit, making them extra vulnerable. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h1)

question: What form of the malaria parasite does a mosquito first inject into a person?

options.A: Merozoites
options.B: Gametocytes
options.C: Zygotes
options.D: Sporozoites

explanation: Correct! Infected mosquitoes carry sporozoites in their salivary glands and inject them right into your skin and blood when they bite. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h2)

question: What happens inside red blood cells to cause those sudden, recurring fever spikes in malaria?

options.A: The rapid multiplication and bursting of red blood cells
options.B: The sudden drop in total white blood cell production
options.C: The allergic reaction to mosquito saliva in the skin
options.D: The physical blocking of large arteries in the heart

explanation: Well done! As the parasites multiply and burst out of red blood cells, they release toxins that trigger a sudden, intense fever. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h2)

question: Which sign tells you a patient has severe malaria instead of just uncomplicated malaria?

options.A: Impaired consciousness or coma
options.B: Loss of appetite
options.C: Mild intermittent headache
options.D: Low-grade joint pain

explanation: Spot on! Any sign of confusion, extreme weakness, or coma (cerebral malaria) means it's an emergency needing immediate inpatient care. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h3)

question: A patient comes to the clinic with a fever and headache, but is fully alert and able to swallow drugs. How do you classify this?

options.A: Asymptomatic malaria
options.B: Chronic malaria
options.C: Severe malaria
options.D: Uncomplicated malaria

explanation: Correct! Because the patient is stable and can take oral meds without danger signs, it's uncomplicated malaria. You'll see this a lot in clinical postings! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h3)

question: Why shouldn't nurses just give anti-malarials immediately to every patient with a fever without testing first?

options.A: RDT kits never work during the rainy season
options.B: Patients refuse to take medications without laboratory proof
options.C: Malaria drugs are too expensive to give out freely
options.D: Many other infections can cause similar symptoms to malaria

explanation: You got it! Illnesses like typhoid or UTIs can also cause fever. Testing first stops us from mistreating patients and wasting precious drugs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h4)

question: What makes a Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) so great for a busy rural health clinic?

options.A: It gives quick results from a finger-prick blood sample without complex equipment
options.B: It permanently prevents future mosquito bites from causing infection
options.C: It is the only test capable of identifying dead parasites after treatment
options.D: It tells the nurse the exact number of parasites circulating in the blood

explanation: Spot on! RDTs are fast, portable, and a lifesaver in clinics where there are no fancy lab machines or steady electricity. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why do we combine two different drugs in Artemisinin-Based Combination Therapy (ACT)?

options.A: To make the medication taste better for young children
options.B: To shorten the treatment duration to a single dose
options.C: To eliminate the need for any laboratory blood testing
options.D: To prevent or delay the development of parasite resistance

explanation: Correct! Teaming up two drugs with different actions helps wipe out all parasites cleanly and stops them from learning how to fight off the medicine. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h5)

question: A patient with severe malaria is admitted to your ward. How should they first receive their medication?

options.A: Oral tablets swallowed with water
options.B: Subcutaneous daily injection
options.C: Rectal suppositories only
options.D: Intravenous or intramuscular

explanation: Well done! Severe cases move fast, so we need fast-acting injections (IV or IM artesunate) to get the drug into their system immediately. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h5)

question: What is the main goal of Intermittent Preventive Treatment in pregnancy (IPTp)?

options.A: To prevent the woman from ever being bitten by a mosquito
options.B: To boost the production of red blood cells in the bone marrow
options.C: To cure a severe case of cerebral malaria in the third trimester
options.D: To clear hidden parasites and protect the mother and baby

explanation: Spot on! IPTp is given during antenatal care to keep pregnant mums and their babies safe from the hidden dangers of malaria. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h6)

question: Why are Insecticide-Treated Nets (ITNs) most effective when used while sleeping?

options.A: Anopheles mosquitoes bite mostly at night when people are asleep
options.B: It prevents mosquitoes from laying eggs inside household water pots
options.C: The chemical on the net repels daytime flies and cockroaches
options.D: It completely stops the flow of humid air into the bedroom

explanation: You got it! Since malaria mosquitoes love to hunt during the night, sleeping under a treated net hits them right when they are most active. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h6)

question: What causes severe anemia in a patient with advanced malaria?

options.A: A complete failure of dietary iron absorption in the gut
options.B: Sudden internal bleeding in the gastrointestinal tract
options.C: Suppression of kidney function leading to blood loss in urine
options.D: Destruction and rapid loss of red blood cells by the parasite

explanation: Correct! As the malaria parasites multiply and break open red blood cells en masse, the patient's blood count drops sharply, causing severe anemia. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h7)

question: An unconscious child with cerebral malaria is brought into the emergency ward. What is your very first nursing priority?

options.A: Ensuring a clear airway and monitoring breathing
options.B: Discharging the patient home with anti-malarial tablets
options.C: Encouraging the mother to feed the child oral porridge
options.D: Checking visual acuity using a Snellen eye chart

explanation: Spot on! ABCs come first in nursing. An unconscious child can easily choke or struggle to breathe, so keeping that airway open is priority number one. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h7)

question: How does health education in the community help reduce malaria cases?

options.A: It empowers families to use preventive tools and seek early testing
options.B: It replaces the need for hospital laboratories in rural zones
options.C: It provides immediate immunity to newborns in endemic regions
options.D: It permanently eliminates mosquito breeding sites nationwide

explanation: Well done! Teaching families how to use nets properly and report fevers early stops infections before they spiral out of control. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h8)

question: Which of these is NOT a standard community prevention message taught by nurses?

options.A: Attending antenatal clinics for preventive treatment during pregnancy
options.B: Sleeping inside insecticide-treated nets every single night
options.C: Taking high doses of antibiotics to prevent malaria infection
options.D: Clearing stagnant water puddles around residential houses

explanation: Correct! Antibiotics fight bacteria, not malaria parasites. Taking them for malaria is incorrect and only builds drug resistance. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T3#GNS214_U1_T3_h8)

question: What specific cells in the human body does HIV primarily attack and destroy?

options.A: CD4+ T-lymphocytes
options.B: Neutrophils
options.C: Red blood cells
options.D: Platelets

explanation: HIV specifically targets and destroys CD4+ T-lymphocytes, which weakens the immune response over time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h1)

question: What is the main difference between HIV and AIDS?

options.A: HIV only affects children whereas AIDS affects adults.
options.B: HIV is transmitted by blood while AIDS is transmitted sexually.
options.C: AIDS can be cured completely with antibiotics unlike HIV.
options.D: AIDS is the advanced stage when the immune system is severely damaged.

explanation: Think of HIV as the virus that enters the body, and AIDS as the later stage when the immune system gets very weak and can no longer fight off sickness. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which enzyme helps HIV convert its viral RNA into DNA inside the host cell?

options.A: Reverse transcriptase
options.B: Amylase
options.C: Pepsin
options.D: DNA polymerase

explanation: HIV uses an enzyme called reverse transcriptase to rewrite its genetic code from RNA into DNA so it can hide inside our body's cells. Clever little virus, but now you know its trick! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h2)

question: Which of the following is NOT a primary mode of HIV transmission?

options.A: Unprotected sexual intercourse with an infected person
options.B: Sharing contaminated needles among drug users
options.C: Casual social contact like hugging and sharing utensils
options.D: Transmission from an infected mother to her baby during birth

explanation: HIV is not spread through everyday casual social contact, sweat, tears, saliva, or insect bites. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h2)

question: What happens during the clinical latency stage of HIV?

options.A: The immune system completely eradicates the virus without treatment.
options.B: The virus multiplies slowly and the patient often feels healthy.
options.C: CD4 cell counts rapidly increase above normal levels.
options.D: The patient experiences severe opportunistic infections immediately.

explanation: During this quiet period, the virus stays active but multiplies slowly. Many patients look and feel completely fine, which is why testing is so important! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h3)

question: A patient is officially diagnosed with AIDS when their CD4 count drops below which threshold?

options.A: 800 cells/mm3
options.B: 200 cells/mm3
options.C: 500 cells/mm3
options.D: 1000 cells/mm3

explanation: A CD4 count falling below 200 cells/mm3 marks the transition from chronic HIV infection to a diagnosis of AIDS. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h3)

question: Within how many hours must Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) be started to work effectively?

options.A: 24 days
options.B: 1 week
options.C: 72 hours
options.D: 1 month

explanation: Time is precious here! PEP needs to start as soon as possible, and ideally within 72 hours after a possible exposure, to stop the virus from taking root. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h4)

question: How does Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) help prevent HIV?

options.A: It is given as a one-time vaccine to provide lifelong immunity.
options.B: It is taken only after a person knows they have been exposed to the virus.
options.C: It kills existing opportunistic infections in AIDS patients.
options.D: It is taken daily by HIV-negative people to block the virus from establishing an infection.

explanation: Think of PrEP as a daily shield. People who are HIV-negative take it regularly to keep the virus from setting up shop if exposure happens. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h4)

question: What does the acronym VCT stand for in HIV nursing care?

options.A: Vaccination and Chemotherapy Therapy
options.B: Voluntary Counseling and Testing
options.C: Viral Care Treatment
options.D: Venereal Control Technique

explanation: VCT stands for Voluntary Counseling and Testing, a core strategy for encouraging people to know their HIV status confidentially. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h5)

question: A patient tests positive for HIV at the clinic. What is your best immediate nursing action?

options.A: Report the patient's name to local community leaders immediately
options.B: Advise the patient to stop working and isolate at home forever
