question: Where are community health nurses most likely to meet families to talk about the value of school?

options.A: Inside high courtrooms during child custody legal proceedings
options.B: During parliamentary budget planning sessions in the capital city
options.C: During home visits, immunization clinics, and community meetings
options.D: At international nursing research conferences held overseas

explanation: Spot on! Routine outreach gives nurses a great chance to chat directly with parents right where they live and gather. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T47#GNS214_U1_T47_h4)

question: A community health nurse notices a 12-year-old girl has suddenly stopped coming to school and clinic. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Ignore the absence since it falls outside routine clinical nursing duties
options.B: Investigate the reason for absence through a home visit or family talk
options.C: Report the family to the international criminal court immediately
options.D: Wait until the end of the year to see if the child returns on her own

explanation: That's right! A sudden dropout is a red flag. Checking in with the family helps you find out what's going on and offer support early. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T47#GNS214_U1_T47_h4)

question: What is a common reason adolescent girls miss or drop out of school once they reach puberty?

options.A: Mandatory government laws prohibiting teenagers from studying science
options.B: Complete lack of interest in academic subjects after primary education
options.C: Sudden loss of intellectual capacity related to biological changes
options.D: Lack of private sanitation facilities and affordable menstrual products

explanation: Sadly, many girls miss classes because their schools lack clean, private toilets or affordable pads to manage their periods comfortably. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T47#GNS214_U1_T47_h5)

question: How do school health programs help keep female students in class?

options.A: By strictly punishing any student who fails a monthly health examination
options.B: By managing hygiene, health screenings, and offering a safe support system
options.C: By providing free uniforms, books, and daily hot meals for all students
options.D: By taking over classroom teaching responsibilities from regular teachers

explanation: Correct! Providing clean facilities, health checks, and a listening ear helps girls feel safe, healthy, and confident to stay in school. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T47#GNS214_U1_T47_h5)

question: Which Nigerian law provides key legal protection against child marriage and stopping a child's education?

options.A: The National Drug Formulary Act
options.B: The Nurses and Midwives Registration Act
options.C: The Child Rights Act
options.D: The Public Health Sanitation Decree

explanation: Spot on! The Child Rights Act is designed to protect children's basic rights, including their right to go to school and be safe from early marriage. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T47#GNS214_U1_T47_h6)

question: Why is it important to involve traditional and religious leaders when promoting girl child education?

options.A: They work exclusively as classroom teachers in secondary boarding schools
options.B: They hold immense influence over local cultural norms and community acceptance
options.C: They are responsible for funding all primary health care clinics in rural areas
options.D: They write the national school curriculum and select all textbook titles

explanation: That's correct! Because local and religious leaders guide community beliefs, having their support makes it much easier to change attitudes and help girls stay in school. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T47#GNS214_U1_T47_h6)

question: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), what age range covers adolescents and youths?

options.A: 5 to 12 years
options.B: 25 to 40 years
options.C: Birth to 5 years
options.D: 10 to 24 years

explanation: You got this! International health guidelines define the adolescent and youth bracket as spanning from 10 to 24 years. It's a vital transition phase you'll see often in community nursing. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h1)

question: Why do standard primary health clinics often struggle to attract young people?

options.A: They charge higher fees for younger patients.
options.B: They only open during school hours.
options.C: They refuse to treat patients without a parent present.
options.D: They are usually structured for either small children or older adults.

explanation: Traditional clinics are often set up for babies (immunizations) or older adults, leaving teenagers feeling awkward and out of place. Great clinics need to feel welcoming to everyone! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h1)

question: Which mental health challenges commonly first show up during the adolescent years?

options.A: Depression and anxiety
options.B: Parkinson's tremors
options.C: Senile cataracts
options.D: Dementia and delirium

explanation: Spot on! Adolescence comes with massive life changes, making it a peak time for mood and emotional shifts like depression and anxiety to emerge. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h2)

question: A 16-year-old girl visits the clinic showing signs of severe mood swings and sudden weight loss. What should you, as the nurse, suspect first?

options.A: Emerging psychosocial or mental health challenges typical of this age group
options.B: Normal age-related cognitive decline
options.C: Permanent physical disability from birth
options.D: Early onset geriatric syndrome

explanation: Well done! Teens experiencing emotional stress often show it through sudden changes in behavior, body image concerns, or physical symptoms. Always keep an eye out for their mental wellbeing. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h2)

question: What is the number one thing that encourages young people to open up and share sensitive health info with a nurse?

options.A: Free mobile phones
options.B: Presence of tribal leaders
options.C: Free meals at the clinic
options.D: Guaranteed confidentiality

explanation: Trust is everything! Teens need to know their secrets are safe with you before they'll feel comfortable talking about their health. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT a core feature of youth-friendly healthcare services?

options.A: Displaying non-judgmental staff attitudes
options.B: Providing affordable or free services
options.C: Demanding parental consent for every minor interaction
options.D: Maintaining strict patient confidentiality

explanation: If a clinic demands parental permission for every little thing, scared teens simply won't come. Youth-friendly care balances guidance with privacy so young people still seek help. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h3)

question: Which vaccine is given in adolescent health programs to protect against cervical cancer later in life?

options.A: Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine
options.B: Oral polio vaccine
options.C: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine
options.D: Tetanus toxoid vaccine

explanation: Exactly! Giving the HPV vaccine to adolescents is a powerful preventive tool against the strains of the virus that cause cervical cancer. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h4)

question: Why do youth health programmes include counseling against substance abuse?

options.A: Substance use is a legal matter handled exclusively by police officers.
options.B: Alcohol and drugs are only used by teenagers.
options.C: Lifestyle habits formed during youth heavily influence long-term health outcomes.
options.D: It is a requirement to receive government funding for equipment.

explanation: Spot on! Habits picked up in the teenage years often stick around. Catching substance use early helps prevent lifelong health struggles. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h4)

question: What is a major social barrier that stops young people from visiting a health clinic?

options.A: Lack of electricity in the clinic waiting room
options.B: Excessive availability of free medication
options.C: Too many books in the facility library
options.D: Fear of being judged or stigmatized by healthcare workers

explanation: Nobody wants to be lectured or looked down on. When health workers show moralizing attitudes, young people stay far away from the clinic. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h5)

question: How can a clinic best handle scheduling barriers for teenagers who are still in school?

options.A: By refusing service to anyone under eighteen years old
options.B: By forcing students to drop out of school to attend clinics
options.C: By closing down clinics entirely during exam weeks
options.D: By offering flexible operating hours and weekend services

explanation: Flexibility is key! Offering weekend or after-school hours ensures students don't have to choose between their education and their health. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h5)

question: What is the best way for a nurse to communicate when talking with a teenager client?

options.A: Speak loudly and use complex Latin terms
options.B: Use simple language without complicated medical jargon
options.C: Write everything down without speaking directly
options.D: Ask parents to answer all questions on behalf of the youth

explanation: Keep it simple and clear! Avoiding heavy medical jargon helps young clients understand their health without feeling intimidated. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h6)

question: How does a nurse act as a true advocate for an adolescent patient?

options.A: By reporting every minor detail of counseling sessions to village elders
options.B: By charging extra fees for confidential consultations
options.C: By restricting access to health information to adults only
options.D: By protecting client confidentiality and defending their right to respectful care

explanation: You got it! As an advocate, you stand up for your young patients' rights to safe, private, and judgment-free care. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h6)

question: Why are peer educators so effective in adolescent health programs?

options.A: They are authorized to write prescriptions for antibiotics
options.B: Peer educators have medical degrees from universities
options.C: Young people often relate better to individuals in their own age group
options.D: Adults refuse to talk to anyone under twenty years old

explanation: Exactly! Teens share the same language and experiences, making peer educators trusted messengers who can easily connect with them. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h7)

question: What is the main reason for involving community and religious leaders in youth health programs?

options.A: To diagnose complex tropical diseases in children
options.B: To prescribe medication during nursing staff shortages
options.C: To build cultural acceptance and reduce community resistance
options.D: To manage the financial accounts of the clinic

explanation: Community leaders hold great influence. Bringing them on board helps secure local backing and prevents cultural pushback against sensitive topics. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h7)

question: What is a direct way to check the quality of youth-friendly services from the clients' own viewpoint?

options.A: Counting the number of chairs in the parking lot
options.B: Gathering feedback through exit interviews and suggestion boxes
options.C: Reading national textbooks on adult medicine
options.D: Checking the personal financial records of the nursing staff

explanation: Spot on! Asking the young clients directly via suggestion boxes or quick chats lets you know what's working and what needs fixing. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h8)

question: A clinic notices a sudden drop in teenagers coming in for counseling. What is the best next step?

options.A: Blame the local school teachers for poor student attendance
options.B: Close the clinic permanently and transfer staff to another district
options.C: Increase user fees to attract a wealthier class of patients
options.D: Investigate possible barriers like staff attitude or operating times through youth feedback

explanation: A drop in numbers is a warning sign. Checking in with the youth helps you pinpoint the problem—whether it's bad staff attitude or inconvenient opening hours—so you can fix it! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T48#GNS214_U1_T48_h8)

question: What is the proper term for healthcare services given to a woman during pregnancy?

options.A: Paediatric surveillance
options.B: Postpartum recovery
options.C: Antenatal care
options.D: Gynecological screening

explanation: Antenatal care (ANC) is simply the medical supervision and support given to an expectant mother throughout her pregnancy. You've got this! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T49#GNS214_U1_T49_h1)

question: Why is antenatal care considered a key preventive service in primary health care?

options.A: It completely prevents all natural discomforts associated with pregnancy.
options.B: It replaces the requirement for skilled attendants during active labor.
options.C: It focuses on detecting health problems before they become severe emergencies.
options.D: It eliminates the need for any medications during the entire gestation period.

explanation: Spotting risks early is the main goal of ANC! Catching little issues before they turn into emergencies keeps both mum and baby safe. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T49#GNS214_U1_T49_h1)

question: How does a pregnant woman's total blood volume usually change during a normal pregnancy?

options.A: It decreases sharply to prevent high blood pressure.
options.B: It remains completely unchanged throughout gestation.
options.C: It increases by nearly half to support the placenta.
options.D: It fluctuates wildly based on daily fluid intake.

explanation: Amazing body fact: a mum's blood volume expands by almost 50% to make sure the baby and placenta get all the blood and oxygen they need! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T49#GNS214_U1_T49_h2)

question: What causes pregnant women to frequently experience constipation and heartburn?

options.A: Expectant mothers consume too much iron too early in the first trimester.
options.B: Increased stomach acid burns away the lining of the small intestine.
options.C: High levels of progesterone slow down smooth muscle movement in the gut.
options.D: The expanding uterus completely shuts down all digestive enzyme production.

explanation: Blame progesterone! This pregnancy hormone relaxes smooth muscles all over the body, which slows down digestion and causes sluggish bowels and acid reflux. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T49#GNS214_U1_T49_h2)

question: Which clinical measurement is used during routine clinic visits to monitor physical fetal growth?

options.A: Fundal height in centimeters
options.B: Maternal weight gain in pounds
options.C: Fetal movement count per hour
options.D: Abdominal girth around the navel

explanation: Measuring fundal height (from the pubic bone to the top of the uterus) gives us a quick, reliable way to check that the baby is growing nicely week by week. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T49#GNS214_U1_T49_h3)

question: A clinic nurse tests a urine sample from a 32-week pregnant woman and finds protein in it. What should the nurse suspect first?

options.A: Gestational hypertension with pre-eclampsia
options.B: Normal physiological kidney adaptation
options.C: Severe iron-deficiency anemia
options.D: Dietary sugar overload from lunch

explanation: Protein in the urine combined with high blood pressure later in pregnancy is a classic warning sign of pre-eclampsia that needs immediate attention. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T49#GNS214_U1_T49_h3)

question: Why is taking folic acid supplements especially critical in the early stages of pregnancy?

options.A: It lowers the mother's resting heart rate during the first trimester.
options.B: It prevents neural tube defects in the developing spine and brain.
options.C: It prevents gestational diabetes from developing later in life.
options.D: It stops severe morning sickness and persistent vomiting.

explanation: Folic acid is a superhero vitamin for early cell division, protecting the baby's developing brain and spinal cord from serious birth defects. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T49#GNS214_U1_T49_h4)

question: What is the main reason iron supplements are routinely given to pregnant women?

options.A: To harden the fetal tooth enamel before delivery occurs
options.B: To prevent anemia caused by expanding blood volume and fetal demands
options.C: To lower maternal blood pressure during the third trimester
options.D: To speed up the digestion of complex proteins in the stomach

explanation: Because a pregnant mum's blood volume shoots up, her body needs extra iron to build all those extra red blood cells without running low. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T49#GNS214_U1_T49_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a danger sign that requires immediate emergency referral during pregnancy?

options.A: Severe, throbbing headache with blurred vision
options.B: Sudden gush or trickle of fluid from the vagina before term
options.C: Mild, occasional dependent ankle swelling at the end of the day
options.D: Bright red vaginal bleeding at any gestational age

explanation: Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day is super common due to extra pressure in the lower body. But bleeding, sudden fluid leakage, and bad headaches are red flags! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T49#GNS214_U1_T49_h5)

question: If an expectant mother reports a sudden decrease in fetal movement, what should you suspect first?

options.A: The fetus has dropped into the pelvic cavity
options.B: The mother is simply too busy to notice kicks
options.C: Normal sleeping patterns of a full-term baby
options.D: Potential fetal distress or oxygen deprivation

explanation: Always take a drop in baby kicks seriously! It can be a vital warning sign that the baby is under distress and needs an urgent check-up. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T49#GNS214_U1_T49_h5)

question: What is the main goal of birth preparedness and complication readiness (BPCR) during antenatal care?

options.A: To train family members to deliver the baby at home safely
options.B: To prevent dangerous delays in reaching emergency obstetric care
options.C: To remove the financial cost of hospital supplies completely
options.D: To guarantee that the baby is born on the exact estimated date

explanation: BPCR is all about planning ahead (transport, funds, blood donors) so that if an emergency strikes, the mother doesn't lose precious time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T49#GNS214_U1_T49_h6)

question: A 36-week pregnant mum asks why the nurse wants her to identify a blood donor and save transport money. How should the nurse reply?

options.A: These steps ensure quick action if an unexpected emergency like heavy bleeding occurs.
options.B: The hospital requires these items as a deposit before admitting any woman in labor.
options.C: Blood donations are used to test your own blood type one final time.
options.D: It is a legal formality that has no real impact on your actual delivery outcome.

explanation: Having cash and a willing blood donor ready beforehand can literally save a life if heavy bleeding (hemorrhage) happens suddenly. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T49#GNS214_U1_T49_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of intra-natal care?

options.A: Achieving a safe delivery for mother and baby
options.B: Ensuring the mother sleeps through delivery
options.C: Speeding up the duration of the first stage
options.D: Preventing the need for any pain relief

explanation: The main focus of intra-natal care is to safeguard the health and well-being of both the mother and the newborn throughout labor and birth. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h1)

question: Why is continuous emotional reassurance important during intra-natal care?

options.A: It replaces the need for physical monitoring of the fetus
options.B: It forces the cervix to dilate much faster
options.C: It lowers anxiety and helps the mother cope with labor pain
options.D: It completely stops the progression of strong contractions

explanation: Emotional support reduces fear and stress hormones, which helps the mother manage the intense physical demands of labor more effectively. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h1)

question: What are the three main components that drive normal labor?

options.A: Placenta, position, and pain
options.B: Pulse, pressure, and pelvis
options.C: Perineum, protein, and pushing
options.D: Passenger, passage, and power

explanation: Labor progress depends entirely on the baby (passenger), the birth canal (passage), and uterine contractions (power). [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h2)

question: What term describes the thinning of the cervix during the first stage of labor?

options.A: Engagement
options.B: Effacement
options.C: Extension
options.D: Descent

explanation: Cervical effacement refers to the shortening and thinning of the cervical canal before and during the dilation process. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h2)

question: When does the second stage of labor end?

options.A: At the onset of true contractions
options.B: When the cervix is fully dilated
options.C: At the birth of the baby
options.D: When the placenta is delivered

explanation: The second stage spans from full cervical dilation all the way until the infant is completely delivered. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h3)

question: A woman has just delivered her baby ten minutes ago, and you are waiting for the placenta to separate. Which stage of labor is she currently in?

options.A: Third stage
options.B: Fourth stage
options.C: First stage
options.D: Second stage

explanation: The third stage of labor begins immediately after the baby is born and lasts until the complete delivery of the placenta. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h3)

question: What is the normal baseline range for the fetal heart rate?

options.A: 60 to 100 beats per minute
options.B: 110 to 160 beats per minute
options.C: 80 to 120 beats per minute
options.D: 140 to 180 beats per minute

explanation: A healthy baseline fetal heart rate consistently falls between 110 and 160 beats per minute during labor. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h4)

question: Why is regular monitoring of maternal blood pressure important during labor?

options.A: To detect pregnancy-induced hypertension or shock early
options.B: To calculate the exact birth weight of the baby
options.C: To determine when the placenta will separate
options.D: To measure how fast the cervix is opening

explanation: Tracking maternal blood pressure helps identify dangerous spikes like preeclampsia or drops indicating bleeding or distress. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h4)

question: At what centimeter of cervical dilation does the plotting of the active phase on a standard partograph typically begin?

options.A: 10 centimeters
options.B: 4 centimeters
options.C: 7 centimeters
options.D: 1 centimeter

explanation: The active phase and routine partograph plotting traditionally commence once the cervix reaches 4 centimeters of dilation. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h5)

question: What does it mean when the cervical dilation curve crosses the action line on a partograph?

options.A: The baby is ready to be delivered immediately
options.B: Labor is progressing faster than normal limits
options.C: Intervention or timely referral is urgently required
options.D: The mother has entered the fourth stage of labor

explanation: Crossing the action line signals prolonged labor, prompting healthcare workers to take corrective action or transfer the patient. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the essential clean delivery practices?

options.A: Clean cutting instrument for the cord
options.B: Clean surgical face mask for every visitor
options.C: Clean surface for the mother to deliver on
options.D: Clean hands of the birth attendant

explanation: The core clean delivery practices focus on hands, delivery surface, perineum, cord cutting tools, and cord ties rather than visitor masks. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h6)

question: Why should the number of routine vaginal examinations be limited during labor?

options.A: To stop the mother from feeling any discomfort
options.B: To make sure contractions do not become too weak
options.C: To reduce the risk of introducing bacteria into the birth canal
options.D: To prevent the baby from moving too quickly down the pelvis

explanation: Each vaginal examination carries a small risk of pushing vaginal flora upward, potentially causing postpartum uterine infections. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h6)

question: What is the primary reason for drying a newborn immediately after birth?

options.A: To stimulate the baby to cry louder
options.B: To check for birth marks on the skin
options.C: To prevent heat loss and hypothermia
options.D: To remove excess vernix completely

explanation: Wet skin combined with evaporation causes rapid heat loss in newborns, making immediate drying essential to prevent cold stress. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h7)

question: A newborn is born limp, pale, and not breathing. What should be your very first immediate action in resuscitation?

options.A: Clear the airway and position the head correctly
options.B: Clamp and cut the cord immediately
options.C: Administer intravenous antibiotics right away
options.D: Weigh the baby on the delivery scale

explanation: Effective resuscitation begins with proper head positioning and clearing the airway to ensure air can enter the lungs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h7)

question: Which position is commonly used to relieve pressure during an umbilical cord prolapse?

options.A: Flat supine position
options.B: Left lateral position only
options.C: Upright sitting position
options.D: Knee-chest position

explanation: Placing the mother in the knee-chest position uses gravity to keep the presenting fetal part off the compressed umbilical cord. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h8)

question: What is the main danger associated with shoulder dystocia during delivery?

options.A: Rapid tearing of the uterine wall at the fundus
options.B: Fetal oxygen deprivation due to trapped shoulders
options.C: Sudden severe infection in the maternal bladder
options.D: Immediate premature separation of the placenta

explanation: When the baby's shoulder gets stuck behind the pubic bone, the umbilical cord can be compressed, cutting off oxygen supply. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h8)

question: When should clinical observations and procedures be documented during labor?

options.A: Only if a complication actually occurs
options.B: Immediately after they are performed
options.C: At the end of the entire nursing shift
options.D: When the patient is discharged home

explanation: Immediate documentation prevents memory lapses and ensures an accurate chronological record of the labor process. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h9)

question: Why is a structured handover important when transferring a patient to the postnatal ward?

options.A: It allows the delivery room staff to take a longer break
options.B: It replaces the need for keeping a written clinical chart
options.C: It forces the patient to retell her entire medical history
options.D: It ensures vital information and ongoing risks are clearly communicated

explanation: A structured handover prevents important clinical details from being missed, ensuring safe continuity of care. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h9)

question: At what specific time intervals is the Apgar score routinely assessed after birth?

options.A: Immediately and thirty minutes
options.B: Ten minutes and twenty minutes
options.C: Two hours and four hours
options.D: One minute and five minutes

explanation: The Apgar score is standardly evaluated at one minute to check how well the baby tolerated birth, and at five minutes to see how well the baby is adapting outside the womb. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h1)

question: What does the 'Grimace' component of the Apgar score actually measure?

options.A: The newborn's facial symmetry
options.B: Reflex irritability to stimulation
options.C: Spontaneous crying duration
options.D: Respiratory muscle effort

explanation: Grimace evaluates how the baby reacts and pulls away or coughs when stimulated, which tells nurses about the state of the nervous system. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h1)

question: What is the main reason newborns frequently develop mild physiological jaundice in the first few days of life?

options.A: Rapid destruction of white blood cells
options.B: An allergic reaction to early breast milk feeds
options.C: Bacterial colonization of the large intestine
options.D: Immature liver enzymes processing red blood cells

explanation: A newborn's liver is still maturing and cannot quickly process the large volume of bilirubin created when extra fetal red blood cells break down. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h2)

question: A healthy newborn is crying vigorously in the delivery room. Which circulatory change is happening to help oxygenate the blood?

options.A: Pulmonary blood vessels constrict to push blood back
options.B: Fetal shunts close to direct blood through the lungs
options.C: Systemic blood pressure drops to zero
options.D: The liver stops receiving blood supply temporarily

explanation: When the baby takes its first breath, lung vessels open up and fetal shunts close so that blood goes directly to the lungs for oxygen. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h2)

question: What does a bulging anterior fontanelle typically indicate during a physical assessment of a newborn?

options.A: Increased intracranial pressure
options.B: Low blood sugar levels
options.C: Normal developmental growth
options.D: Mild systemic dehydration

explanation: A tight, bulging soft spot on a baby's head is a warning sign that pressure inside the skull is higher than normal. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h3)

question: Which finding is considered a normal part of confirming lower gastrointestinal patency in a newborn?

options.A: A loud cry during diaper changes
options.B: Passing the first meconium stool
options.C: Vomiting greenish amniotic fluid
options.D: Passing clear watery urine

explanation: The passage of meconium proves that the lower digestive tract is open and working correctly from top to bottom. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h3)

question: How do newborns primarily generate body heat when they are exposed to cold environments?

options.A: Rhythmic skeletal muscle shivering
options.B: Metabolizing brown adipose tissue
options.C: Sweating through specialized skin pores
options.D: Rapid increase in respiratory rate

explanation: Unlike adults, newborns cannot shiver well; instead, they burn special brown fat stores to create and maintain body heat. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h4)

question: Why is delayed bathing recommended for stable newborns immediately after birth?

options.A: It allows the umbilical cord stump to dry
options.B: It helps preserve vernix for skin immunity
options.C: It prevents early neonatal jaundice spikes
options.D: It prevents rapid heat loss and cold stress

explanation: Washing a wet baby too soon strips away heat through evaporation, putting them at high risk for dangerous drops in body temperature. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h4)

question: What is the recommended approach for routine daily care of a normal umbilical cord stump?

options.A: Washing with harsh antibacterial soaps daily
options.B: Covering it tightly with an adhesive bandage
options.C: Keeping it clean, dry, and exposed to air
options.D: Applying heavy petroleum jelly dressings

explanation: Keeping the cord dry and open to air helps it shrivel and fall off quickly while preventing bacterial growth. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h5)

question: Which clinical observation around the umbilical stump indicates the development of omphalitis?

options.A: Redness of the skin and foul-smelling discharge
options.B: A dry, black, and completely shriveled stump
options.C: Natural separation of the cord after one week
options.D: A small drop of clear blood upon diaper removal

explanation: Spreading redness, swelling, and pus or bad smells around the navel are classic signs of a dangerous umbilical infection. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h5)

question: What is the primary immunological benefit of early colostrum feeding for a newborn?

options.A: Lowering infant red blood cell destruction rates
options.B: Supplying complete proteins for muscle growth
options.C: Providing high concentrations of secretory IgA antibodies
options.D: Preventing the development of physiological jaundice

explanation: Colostrum is packed with antibodies that coat the baby's digestive tract, protecting them from harmful bacteria and viruses. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h6)

question: Why is ensuring a deep latch crucial during early breastfeeding sessions?

options.A: It prevents maternal nipple pain and ensures milk transfer
options.B: It triggers immediate passage of meconium stools
options.C: It stops the baby from swallowing excess air bubbles
options.D: It keeps the baby's body temperature stable

explanation: A deep latch puts the milk ducts in the baby's mouth rather than just the nipple, protecting the mother from damage while getting milk out effectively. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h6)

question: Why is an intramuscular injection of Vitamin K given routinely to all newborns?

options.A: To prevent dangerous bleeding disorders
options.B: To boost immediate antibody production
options.C: To treat congenital eye infections
options.D: To protect against bacterial meningitis

explanation: Newborn guts are sterile and cannot make Vitamin K yet, so an injection stops life-threatening bleeding complications. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of applying antibiotic eye ointment to a newborn shortly after birth?

options.A: Reducing swelling from bright delivery room lights
options.B: Lubricating dry corneas during the transition period
options.C: Treating severe congenital cataracts and glaucoma
options.D: Preventing ophthalmia neonatorum from birth canal exposure

explanation: Eye ointment protects the infant's eyes from harmful bacteria like gonorrhea and chlamydia picked up while passing through the birth canal. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h7)

question: Which clinical sign is a classic indicator of respiratory distress in a newborn?

options.A: Strong, rhythmic sucking reflexes
options.B: Regular, deep, quiet breathing
options.C: A pink, warm skin appearance
options.D: Intercostal chest retractions

explanation: When a baby struggles to breathe, the skin and muscles around the ribs pull inward noticeably with each breath. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h8)

question: Why is jaundice that appears within the first twenty-four hours of birth considered dangerous?

options.A: It shows that the baby is suffering from severe dehydration
options.B: It indicates that Vitamin K was not given at birth
options.C: It is pathological and points to serious underlying problems
options.D: It means the baby is drinking too much breast milk

explanation: Normal jaundice appears later; jaundice on day one is usually caused by blood group mismatches or severe liver issues needing urgent care. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T51#GNS214_U1_T51_h8)

question: How long does the post-natal period (puerperium) typically last in clinical practice?

options.A: Six months
options.B: Two weeks
options.C: Six weeks
options.D: Three months

explanation: You'll see this time and again in midwifery! The post-natal period is officially defined as the first six weeks after childbirth when the mother's body returns to its pre-pregnant state. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h1)

question: Why is post-natal care just as crucial as the care a mother gets during pregnancy?

options.A: Many serious health complications happen during the weeks after delivery.
options.B: The baby no longer needs any medical attention after birth.
options.C: Hormones return to normal instantly without any professional help.
options.D: It gives the mother time to rest away from her family members.

explanation: Spotting issues early saves lives! A large percentage of maternal and newborn complications happen right after birth, which is why close monitoring during the post-natal phase is a total lifesaver. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h1)

question: For a mother who had a safe, normal delivery, when should her very first post-natal check happen?

options.A: Exactly on the fourteenth day
options.B: Within 24 hours of birth
options.C: After six months
options.D: At the end of the second week

explanation: That first check within 24 hours is super important to catch immediate issues like heavy bleeding or shock before they become emergencies. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h2)

question: When is the final routine post-natal visit usually scheduled to ensure the reproductive organs have fully recovered?

options.A: After one year
options.B: At 24 hours
options.C: On day 3
options.D: Between 4 and 6 weeks

explanation: The 4 to 6-week mark wraps up the puerperium! It's the perfect time for you to confirm the womb has gone back to normal size and chat about family planning. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h2)

question: What do we call the normal vaginal discharge that a mother passes as her uterus heals after birth?

options.A: Lochia
options.B: Colostrum
options.C: Leukorrhea
options.D: Smegma

explanation: Lochia is just the body's natural way of cleaning out the uterus after delivery—shedding old tissue and blood as healing takes place. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h3)

question: What color should a healthy mother's lochia look like during the first three days after delivery?

options.A: Bright red color
options.B: Clear watery consistency
options.C: Green foul-smelling discharge
options.D: Creamy white color

explanation: In the beginning, lochia is called 'rubra' (red) because it's mostly fresh blood and tissue. Completely normal for the first few days! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h3)

question: When you gently feel (palpate) a mother's tummy to check her uterus after birth, what is your main goal?

options.A: To confirm that the uterus is firm and contracting
options.B: To check if the bladder is completely empty
options.C: To stimulate milk production in the breasts
options.D: To measure the exact weight of the mother

explanation: A nice, hard, contracted uterus (like a firm mango!) stops bleeding. If it feels soft or boggy, that's a red flag for postpartum hemorrhage. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h4)

question: On day four, a new mother complains that her right calf is suddenly painful, swollen, and warm to the touch. What should pop into your head first?

options.A: Deep vein thrombosis
options.B: Uterine subinvolution
options.C: Postpartum blues
options.D: Normal postpartum fatigue

explanation: Pain and swelling in just one leg after childbirth is a classic warning sign of a blood clot (DVT). Always take this seriously and report it immediately! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h4)

question: At what exact times after birth is a newborn's Apgar score routinely checked?

options.A: One and five minutes
options.B: Twelve and twenty-four hours
options.C: Ten and twenty minutes
options.D: One and six hours

explanation: Think '1 and 5'! The 1-minute score shows how the baby handled the stress of birth, while the 5-minute score shows how well they are adapting to life outside the womb. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h5)

question: Why do midwives give a routine injection of Vitamin K to newborns shortly after delivery?

options.A: To improve digestion of breastmilk
options.B: To build strong bones and teeth
options.C: To protect against childhood infections
options.D: To prevent dangerous bleeding disorders

explanation: Babies are born with very low levels of Vitamin K and sterile tummies, which puts them at risk of bleeding until their gut flora kicks in. The injection protects them safely! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h5)

question: What is the leading cause of heavy bleeding right after childbirth (early postpartum hemorrhage)?

options.A: High blood pressure
options.B: Excessive walking
options.C: Vitamin deficiency
options.D: Uterine atony

explanation: Uterine atony simply means the womb muscle is too tired to clamp down tightly after delivery. Keeping it firm is a key part of your nursing care! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h6)

question: What is the safest way for a new mother to clean her perineal area after using the toilet?

options.A: Soaking in soapy bathwater
options.B: Washing from back to front
options.C: Washing from front to back
options.D: Wiping vigorously with dry paper

explanation: Front to back always! This golden rule keeps germs from the anal area away from the vagina and urethra, protecting her from nasty infections. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h7)

question: Why must breastfeeding mothers make sure they drink plenty of extra fluids every day?

options.A: To replace fluids lost through breastmilk production
options.B: To flush out the kidneys and stop weight gain
options.C: To help the lochia turn white faster
options.D: To prevent the uterus from contracting too fast

explanation: Breastmilk is mostly water! If mom doesn't drink enough, her milk supply can drop and she can easily become dehydrated. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h7)

question: Which family planning pill is best for mothers who are breastfeeding in the early months because it won't dry up their milk?

options.A: Menopausal hormone therapy
options.B: Combined estrogen pills
options.C: High-dose emergency pills
options.D: Progestin-only pills

explanation: Progestin-only pills (the 'minipill') are safe for nursing moms because they don't mess with breastmilk production like estrogen can. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h8)

question: What is the main health benefit of encouraging child spacing through family planning after having a baby?

options.A: It gives the mother's body time to recover its nutrient stores and strength.
options.B: It makes uterine involution happen within twenty-four hours.
options.C: It guarantees that the next baby will be a male child.
options.D: It completely stops all postpartum mood changes.

explanation: Pregnancy takes a lot out of a woman's body! Spacing pregnancies gives her time to rebuild her iron and nutrient levels so she stays strong for herself and her family. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h8)

question: What is one of the main responsibilities of community health workers when it comes to post-natal care?

options.A: Performing major surgical repairs for tears
options.B: Delivering babies in primary operating theatres
options.C: Conducting home visits and tracking immunizations
options.D: Prescribing strong antibiotics for severe sepsis

explanation: Community health workers are fantastic bridges to the community. They visit homes to make sure babies get their vaccines and moms are recovering nicely. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h9)

question: Why are home visits by community health workers so helpful for new mothers?

options.A: It replaces the need for any professional hospital assessment.
options.B: It prevents the mother from experiencing any fatigue.
options.C: It ensures the baby starts walking much earlier.
options.D: It reaches mothers who might not return to the clinic for check-ups.

explanation: Not every mother can make it back to the clinic due to distance or traditions. Community outreach ensures these mothers aren't left stranded with hidden health issues. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h9)

question: What is the main goal of family planning?

options.A: Permanently stopping population growth in rural areas
options.B: Deciding the number and spacing of children
options.C: Ensuring every woman gives birth in a hospital
options.D: Treating all known sexually transmitted infections

explanation: Spot on! Family planning simply helps couples and individuals choose how many kids they want and the best time to have them. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h1)

question: Which of these is NOT part of routine family planning services?

options.A: Adolescent reproductive health education
options.B: Infertility management and counseling
options.C: Provision of modern contraceptive methods
options.D: Performing major abdominal surgeries

explanation: You got it! Family planning clinics focus on counseling, birth control, and fertility support—not major operations like removing an appendix. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h1)

question: What is the minimum recommended interval between pregnancies to protect maternal and child health?

options.A: At least two years
options.B: Exactly six months
options.C: Three to four weeks
options.D: At least five years

explanation: Spacing pregnancies by at least two years gives the mother's body enough time to recover and lowers infant health risks. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h2)

question: A nursing mother visits the clinic 6 months after delivery. Why is birth spacing important for her next pregnancy?

options.A: It prevents the infant from developing childhood illnesses
options.B: It allows her body and nutrient stores to fully recover
options.C: It guarantees that the next child will have no health issues
options.D: It eliminates the need for antenatal care later

explanation: Exactly! Giving the body a break restores vital nutrients like iron so the mother is strong and ready for the next pregnancy. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h2)

question: Which of the following is classified as a barrier method of contraception?

options.A: Male and female condoms
options.B: Copper intrauterine device
options.C: Progestin-only injectable
options.D: Basal body temperature tracking

explanation: Condoms act as physical barriers that prevent sperm from entering the female reproductive tract. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h3)

question: How do combined hormonal contraceptive pills mainly prevent pregnancy?

options.A: By creating a permanent blockage in the fallopian tubes
options.B: By destroying sperm cells on contact
options.C: By causing early shedding of the womb lining every week
options.D: By stopping ovulation and thickening cervical mucus

explanation: Well done! These hormones trick the body into not releasing an egg while also making it hard for sperm to swim through. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h3)

question: What is your main role as a nurse during family planning counseling?

options.A: To enforce government population targets
options.B: To convince every young person to get sterilized
options.C: To provide clear information so the client can choose freely
options.D: To choose the best contraceptive method for the client

explanation: Correct! As nurses, we guide and educate without forcing our personal choices on our patients. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h4)

question: A client wants a specific pill, but it is unsafe for her because she has severe high blood pressure. What should you do first?

options.A: Give her the requested pill anyway to make her happy
options.B: Send her straight to a big teaching hospital for surgery
options.C: Scold her for choosing a bad medication without asking
options.D: Explain the health risk gently and discuss safer options

explanation: You got it! Patient safety comes first. We calmly explain why a drug isn't safe and gladly help them pick a better alternative. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h4)

question: What infection prevention practice is most important when inserting a contraceptive implant under the skin?

options.A: Giving the patient general anesthesia
options.B: Using strict aseptic (sterile) technique
options.C: Making the patient fast for 12 hours
options.D: Using ultraviolet room lights

explanation: Spot on! Even though it's a minor procedure, keeping everything strictly sterile protects your patient from nasty wound infections. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h5)

question: Why is keeping a proper inventory of family planning supplies so important at a clinic?

options.A: It ensures expired drugs get handed out very fast
options.B: It means you don't have to write daily attendance records
options.C: It lets the nurse sell extra supplies for side cash
options.D: It stops stock-outs so clients don't suddenly run out of their method

explanation: Great thinking! Running out of supplies leaves patients stranded and unprotected, so tracking inventory keeps care running smoothly. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h5)

question: Which side effect is very common with progestin-only injectable contraceptives (like Depo-Provera)?

options.A: Permanent complete hair loss
options.B: Changes in menstrual bleeding patterns
options.C: Sudden swelling of the thyroid gland
options.D: Instant weight loss of 20kg

explanation: Correct! Injectables often change how periods look—some spotting, heavier days, or periods stopping completely are quite normal. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h6)

question: A client comes back complaining of mild spotting a month after getting an implant. How should you respond?

options.A: Tell her she has a serious pelvic infection
options.B: Take out the implant immediately and offer nothing else
options.C: Reassure her that this is a normal and common side effect
options.D: Tell her to stop drinking water for two days

explanation: Spot on! Pre-counseling helps clients stay calm. Reassuring them that spotting is normal builds great trust and keeps them comfortable. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h6)

question: What is a common myth that stops people from using family planning in many communities?

options.A: Family planning guarantees you will have a baby boy
options.B: Contraceptives are made only by local farmers
options.C: Using a condom cures all infections instantly
options.D: Modern contraceptives cause permanent infertility

explanation: You nailed it! A lot of people fear that using birth control now means they won't be able to bear children later, which isn't true. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h7)

question: You notice women in a village want birth control but are scared of their husbands' reactions. What should be your main step?

options.A: Give out contraceptives in secret without telling anyone
options.B: Report all the husbands to the nearest police station
options.C: Organize community talks to involve men in reproductive health education
options.D: Close the clinic until the village changes its culture

explanation: Brilliant approach! Bringing men into the conversation clears up myths, reduces home conflicts, and builds teamwork for family health. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h7)

question: What is the main goal of an Infant Welfare Clinic?

options.A: Emergency trauma management
options.B: Surgical operations for newborns
options.C: Preventive care and health promotion
options.D: Inpatient hospital admission

explanation: You've got this! These clinics focus on stopping illnesses before they start through check-ups and immunizations, rather than treating severe hospital emergencies. Great job keeping kids healthy! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h1)

question: Why are Infant Welfare Clinics usually set up right inside primary health care centres?

options.A: To provide specialized pediatric surgery units
options.B: To isolate sick children from the general population
options.C: To bring preventive services closer to local communities
options.D: To reduce the workload of tertiary teaching hospitals

explanation: Spot on! Placing clinics in local primary health care centres brings essential services right to the grassroots, making it super easy for families to attend routine check-ups. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h1)

question: Which of these is NOT a service you would normally see at an infant welfare clinic?

options.A: Nutritional counseling for mothers
options.B: Growth and weight monitoring
options.C: Routine childhood immunization
options.D: Major orthopedic surgery

explanation: Correct! Major surgeries need advanced hospital theaters, while infant welfare clinics focus purely on basic, everyday preventive care and health education. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h2)

question: A mother brings her healthy six-month-old baby to the clinic. What services should she get today?

options.A: Dental extraction and eye surgery
options.B: Emergency malaria treatment and blood transfusion
options.C: Surgical screening and X-ray imaging
options.D: Growth check, scheduled vaccines, and weaning advice

explanation: Well done! A healthy six-month-old needs a quick weight check, their due immunizations, and a friendly chat about starting solid foods (weaning). [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h2)

question: What simple tool do nurses use to plot a child's weight against their age during clinic visits?

options.A: Patient temperature log
options.B: Road to Health chart
options.C: Blood pressure record sheet
options.D: Surgical safety checklist

explanation: You nailed it! The Road to Health chart is a handy visual tool we use everywhere to track how well a child is growing over time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h3)

question: What does a flattening weight curve on a child's growth chart usually mean first?

options.A: Normal physical growth for that specific age
options.B: An early warning sign of a developing problem
options.C: A measurement error by the attending nurse
options.D: A sudden increase in daily physical activity

explanation: Spot on! When the weight line flattens out, it's often the very first clue that nutrition or health is slipping, even before the child looks visibly thin. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h3)

question: How do vaccines work to protect a child's body against infections?

options.A: By stimulating the immune system to produce antibodies
options.B: By coating the stomach lining to block germ absorption
options.C: By increasing the body temperature to kill viruses
options.D: By providing immediate chemical destruction of all bacteria

explanation: Exactly! Vaccines introduce safe, weakened parts of a germ to train the immune system so it knows how to fight back if the real disease ever shows up. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h4)

question: A mother is worried that routine immunizations will make her baby sick with a fever. What is the best way to reassure her?

options.A: Tell her that vaccines contain dangerous live disease organisms
options.B: Suggest she waits until the child starts school before vaccinating
options.C: Advise her to skip all future injections to keep the baby safe
options.D: Explain that mild fever is a normal sign the body is building immunity

explanation: You got it! A low-grade fever or soreness just means the baby's immune system is actively working out and building strong protection. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h4)

question: For how many months should an infant be exclusively breastfed, according to health guidelines?

options.A: First twelve months
options.B: First nine months
options.C: First three months
options.D: First six months

explanation: Spot on! Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months gives a baby all the water and nourishment they need—no extra water or food required yet! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h5)

question: Why do babies need other foods (complementary feeding) introduced around six months of age?

options.A: Breast milk alone can no longer meet all growing nutritional needs
options.B: Babies automatically reject breast milk once teeth begin to erupt
options.C: Maternal antibodies completely disappear from the mother's milk
options.D: The baby stops producing digestive enzymes for milk proteins

explanation: Correct! As babies grow fast at this stage, they need extra iron and energy that breast milk alone can't fully cover anymore. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h5)

question: Which sign is a major red flag for pneumonia or a serious chest infection in an infant?

options.A: Swollen joints and painful movement
options.B: Yellow discoloration of the skin
options.C: Inability to close the eyelids fully
options.D: Fast breathing or chest indrawing

explanation: Well done! Breathing very fast or having the skin suck in around the ribs are classic warning signs that a baby is struggling to breathe. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h6)

question: A mother brings in her baby who has had watery diarrhea for two days, looks very sleepy (lethargic), and has sunken eyes. What is your immediate nursing priority?

options.A: Measure the child's height and head circumference
options.B: Administer a routine measles vaccine immediately
options.C: Send the mother home with advice to wait another week
options.D: Assess hydration status and prepare for urgent medical referral

explanation: Spot on! Lethargy and sunken eyes mean severe dehydration, which can turn dangerous very quickly. They need urgent fluid care and a doctor's help right away. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h6)

question: What is a major reason why mothers in rural areas struggle to attend infant welfare clinics?

options.A: Mandatory fees that exceed hospital costs
options.B: Long distance and lack of transport
options.C: Excessive availability of private doctors
options.D: Strict laws prohibiting clinic visits

explanation: You got it! Living far away with bad transport options makes it really tough for rural mums to travel to a clinic regularly. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h7)

question: Why do health teams run mobile clinics and community outreach programs?

options.A: To train people to become certified physicians
options.B: To reach populations living far from permanent health facilities
options.C: To replace traditional hospitals permanently
options.D: To collect taxes from rural farming communities

explanation: Correct! Mobile clinics bridge the gap by taking healthcare services right to the doorsteps of remote villages that lack permanent clinics. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h7)

question: What is the main reason we monitor a child's growth at the clinic?

options.A: To detect growth problems before visible signs appear
options.B: To treat children who already have severe infections
options.C: To vaccinate children against common childhood illnesses
options.D: To provide free food supplies to low-income families

explanation: Spotting small changes in weight or height early lets you step in and help before severe malnutrition sets in. You've got this! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h1)

question: Why do we track a child's growth over several visits rather than relying on just one measurement?

options.A: It prevents errors made by community health volunteers
options.B: It shows the direction and velocity of growth over time
options.C: It guarantees the child will not contract infectious diseases
options.D: It is required by government health insurance policies

explanation: A single visit only tells you about today. Tracking over time shows the true pattern—whether the child is growing well or falling behind. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h1)

question: If a young child has a low height-for-age, what does this usually tell us?

options.A: Temporary fluid retention
options.B: Normal genetic short stature
options.C: Chronic or long-term malnutrition
options.D: Sudden weight loss from diarrhea

explanation: Height takes time to change, so a low height-for-age points to long-term nutritional challenges or repeated illnesses over time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h2)

question: A child suddenly loses a lot of weight over two weeks. Which measurement will drop first?

options.A: Weight-for-length
options.B: Body mass index
options.C: Head circumference
options.D: Height-for-age

explanation: Weight changes fast during short-term illness or food shortages, making weight-for-length our best early warning sign for sudden wasting. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h2)

question: What is the correct tool to measure the length of a 14-month-old child?

options.A: A flexible cloth tape measure
options.B: A vertical wall stadiometer
options.C: A hanging spring balance scale
options.D: An infantometer for recumbent length

explanation: Kids under two can't stand straight yet, so we use a flat measuring board (infantometer) while they lie down. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h3)

question: Why should a nurse adjust the weighing scale to zero before weighing every child?

options.A: To make the scale display readings in kilograms instead of pounds
options.B: To comply with international manufacturer warranties
options.C: To calm the child down before the measurement process begins
options.D: To prevent small errors from accumulating between readings

explanation: Always zeroing your scale clears any leftover weight from the previous patient, keeping your numbers accurate every time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h3)

question: How can a nurse prevent reading errors (parallax errors) when using a weighing scale?

options.A: Reading the scale directly at eye level
options.B: Using a digital scale instead of an analog one
options.C: Weighing the child twice and taking the average
options.D: Calibrating the scale with a known standard weight

explanation: Looking at the dial or screen from above or the side can skew your reading. Always position your eyes straight in front of the display! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h4)

question: When measuring the length of a 10-month-old infant, what should you do with their legs?

options.A: Gently press the knees down so the legs lie flat against the board
options.B: Leave the knees relaxed and bent naturally in a frog position
options.C: Wrap both ankles tightly together with a soft bandage
options.D: Lift the legs upward at a 45-degree angle to stretch the spine

explanation: If the knees are bent, your measurement will be shorter than reality. Gently hold the knees flat against the board for an accurate length. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h4)

question: On a standard WHO growth chart, what does the bottom (horizontal) line represent?

options.A: The weight of the child
options.B: The age of the child
options.C: The mid-upper arm circumference
options.D: The height of the child

explanation: Think of the horizontal axis as time passing (age), while the vertical axis shows the measurement like weight or height. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h5)

question: What does it mean when a child's plotted dots form a line pointing upward, running parallel to the reference curves?

options.A: Normal, healthy physical growth
options.B: Immediate risk of severe acute malnutrition
options.C: An error in the initial birth weight record
options.D: Chronic stunting due to repeated infections

explanation: When the curve follows the expected upward path, it's a great sign that the child is gaining weight and growing steadily! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h5)

question: What does 'growth faltering' look like on a child's growth chart?

options.A: A steady upward curve parallel to reference lines
options.B: Measurements that stay above the median line
options.C: A sudden increase in height over one month
options.D: A flat or downward-sloping growth curve

explanation: Growth faltering happens when weight gain slows down or stops entirely, making the growth line flatten out or dip downwards. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h6)

question: Why is it an urgent concern if a child's weight line crosses downward across Z-score lines?

options.A: It indicates normal seasonal weight loss in toddlers
options.B: It means the mother has stopped bringing the child to the clinic
options.C: It shows an active deterioration in nutritional status
options.D: It proves the weighing scale was broken during the visit

explanation: Crossing downward means the child is actively losing ground toward malnutrition and needs quick clinical attention. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a common cause of growth faltering in infants?

options.A: Regular daily physical exercise
options.B: Frequent bouts of childhood diarrhea
options.C: Inadequate complementary feeding
options.D: Recurrent malarial infections

explanation: Normal baby movement doesn't cause faltering. Illness, infections, and poor feeding are the real culprits behind slowed growth. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h7)

question: How do recurring illnesses like malaria lead to childhood malnutrition?

options.A: By directly destroying the child's bone marrow and skeleton
options.B: By changing the color of breast milk in the mother's body
options.C: By forcing the child to sleep longer hours during the day
options.D: By increasing nutrient demand while reducing the child's appetite

explanation: Fever and sickness make the body burn more energy, but sick kids usually don't want to eat. That combination leads straight to weight loss. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h7)

question: What is the best way to start counselling a mother whose child is experiencing growth faltering?

options.A: Tell the mother to stop coming to the clinic until next year
options.B: Ask open-ended questions about recent feeding and illness
options.C: Scold the mother for failing to feed the child properly
options.D: Write a prescription for expensive imported vitamin supplements

explanation: Great nursing starts with empathy and listening. Ask gentle, open questions to understand what's happening at home without judging. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h8)

question: A toddler is showing growth faltering. What is the most practical nutrition advice to give the mother?

options.A: Stop all breastfeeding immediately and switch entirely to cow milk
options.B: Only feed the child imported baby cereals bought from supermarkets
options.C: Reduce the number of daily meals to allow the child's stomach to rest
options.D: Use available local food items to make nutrient-dense meals given more frequently

explanation: Keep advice practical! Recommend affordable, locally available foods that the family can easily prepare and feed the child more often. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h8)

question: How many loose or watery stools in a day is officially considered diarrhoea?

options.A: Passing hard stool once every three days
options.B: Constant abdominal pain with nausea
options.C: Three or more loose or watery stools in a day
options.D: A single episode of bloody stool

explanation: Great job keeping it simple! Diarrhoea is defined as passing three or more loose or watery stools within 24 hours. You'll see this often in clinical practice. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h1)

question: In secretory diarrhoea, why do patients lose water so quickly?

options.A: The liver fails to produce bile acids for digestion
options.B: Intestinal cells actively pump excessive water into the gut lumen
options.C: Stomach acid production increases to dangerous levels
options.D: The kidneys stop filtering waste products completely

explanation: Think of it like an open tap! Toxins trick the cells in the intestines into pushing out lots of water and salt into the gut faster than the body can absorb it. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h1)

question: Which virus is the most common cause of severe, watery diarrhoea in babies?

options.A: Influenza virus
options.B: Varicella zoster
options.C: Hepatitis A
options.D: Rotavirus

explanation: Rotavirus is well-known as the leading viral culprit behind severe dehydrating diarrhoea in infants worldwide. Vaccination has been a game-changer here! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h2)

question: Why does stopping breastfeeding early increase a baby's chance of getting diarrhoea?

options.A: It stops the liver from storing adequate iron reserves
options.B: It forces the infant to produce too much stomach acid
options.C: It causes immediate permanent damage to the pancreas
options.D: It removes protective maternal antibodies that guard the infant gut

explanation: Breast milk is liquid gold for babies! It carries special antibodies that shield their delicate digestive system from germs while their own immune system is still growing. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h2)

question: Which of these is a major warning sign of severe dehydration in a sick child?

options.A: Flushed skin that feels hot to the touch
options.B: An unusually loud and constant cry
options.C: Swelling in both lower legs and feet
options.D: Lethargy or unconsciousness with sunken eyes

explanation: When a child is severely dehydrated, they lose so much fluid that they become very weak, drowsy, or even unconscious, with noticeably sunken eyes. This is an emergency! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h3)

question: A toddler with diarrhoea drinks eagerly from a cup and seems restless. How would you grade this?

options.A: Severe dehydration
options.B: No dehydration
options.C: Some dehydration
options.D: Chronic dehydration

explanation: Spot on! When a child drinks eagerly and is a bit restless or irritable, it's a classic sign of moderate ('some') dehydration. They are thirsty and ready for ORS! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h3)

question: What is the main job of glucose inside Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS)?

options.A: It masks the salty taste of the solution for infants
options.B: It slows down the movement of food through the stomach
options.C: It provides all the daily calories a sick child needs
options.D: It helps transport sodium and water across the intestinal wall

explanation: It's like a buddy system! Glucose hitches a ride with sodium and water, pulling them across the intestinal wall back into the bloodstream to stop dehydration. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h4)

question: Why do we give zinc supplements to a child with diarrhoea?

options.A: It acts as a strong sedative to help the child sleep
options.B: It shortens the illness duration and repairs gut tissue
options.C: It kills bacteria directly in the stomach lining
options.D: It immediately stops all vomiting within one hour

explanation: Zinc is a helper mineral! It helps the gut lining heal faster, boosts immunity, and cuts down how long the child will suffer from diarrhoea. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h4)

question: Why is starving or withholding food from a child with diarrhoea a bad idea?

options.A: It stops the kidneys from producing urine
options.B: It triggers immediate bacterial overgrowth
options.C: It delays gut healing and worsens malnutrition
options.D: It causes the child to vomit up all remaining water

explanation: Old myths die hard, but we know better now! Restricting food starves the gut cells, making it harder for the intestines to repair themselves and leading to weight loss. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h5)

question: What is the best feeding advice for a breastfed baby who gets diarrhoea?

options.A: Continue breastfeeding on demand without interruption
options.B: Wait twenty-four hours before offering breast milk again
options.C: Dilute breast milk with equal parts sterile water
options.D: Stop breastfeeding and switch to plain water only

explanation: Keep feeding! Breast milk gives the baby both hydration and essential nutrients to fight off the infection and stay strong. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h5)

question: Which situation means a child needs intravenous (IV) fluids right away?

options.A: Low-grade fever lasting less than an hour
options.B: A slight decrease in daily appetite
options.C: Mild loose stool passed twice in one day
options.D: Severe dehydration with signs of shock

explanation: When shock and severe dehydration set in, drinking isn't enough anymore. IV fluids are urgently needed to restore blood pressure and save the day. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h6)

question: Why must a nurse monitor a child closely while they receive rapid IV fluids?

options.A: To prevent dangerous fluid overload and watch urine output
options.B: To test the blood glucose levels every five minutes
options.C: To make sure the IV pole is tall enough for gravity
options.D: To calculate the exact caloric intake from the saline

explanation: Balance is everything in nursing. We watch closely to make sure we are rehydrating them safely without flooding their system or straining their kidneys. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h6)

question: Which vaccine directly helps prevent a leading cause of childhood diarrhoea?

options.A: Tetanus toxoid vaccine
options.B: Hepatitis B vaccine
options.C: BCG tuberculosis vaccine
options.D: Rotavirus vaccine

explanation: Prevention is key! The rotavirus vaccine protects little ones from the most common viral bug that causes severe, dehydrating tummy bugs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h7)

question: What is the best way for a community nurse to stop the spread of diarrhoea in a village?

options.A: Providing mosquito nets for sleeping areas at night
options.B: Teaching proper handwashing with soap and safe water storage
options.C: Inspecting local houses for structural roof damage
options.D: Distributing high-dose antibiotic capsules to all households

explanation: Diarrhoea germs usually spread through the faecal-oral route via dirty hands and water. Simple hygiene education and clean water storage save lives! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h7)

question: What is the biggest danger when a young child has acute watery diarrhoea?

options.A: Rapid loss of body fluids and electrolytes
options.B: Permanent damage to the intestinal lining
options.C: Complete loss of appetite for solid food
options.D: Severe systemic bacterial infection

explanation: You nailed it! When a child has watery diarrhoea, water and vital salts rush out of the body very quickly, which can lead to dangerous dehydration. Catching this early makes all the difference! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T57#GNS214_U1_T57_h1)

question: Why does severe dehydration eventually cause organs to stop working in a child?

options.A: Electrolyte imbalances cause immediate paralysis of the heart
options.B: The kidneys stop working because they are overworked by toxins
options.C: Reduced blood volume leads to poor oxygen delivery to tissues
options.D: The digestive tract bursts from lack of internal pressure

explanation: Think of blood like a delivery truck carrying oxygen. When water is lost, total blood volume drops, meaning vital organs don't get the oxygen they need to keep running smoothly. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T57#GNS214_U1_T57_h1)

question: What is the main goal of giving Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT)?

options.A: To stop the bowels from moving immediately
options.B: To replace lost fluids and electrolytes using the gut
options.C: To kill the bacteria causing the stomach infection
options.D: To provide full daily nutritional calories

explanation: Spot on! ORT uses the body's natural drinking process to safely put back all the water and essential mineral salts that were washed away. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T57#GNS214_U1_T57_h2)

question: How does adding a little glucose to oral rehydration solution help the body absorb water?

options.A: Glucose creates a thick barrier that stops water from leaving the body
options.B: Glucose binds with sodium to pull water across the gut wall together
options.C: Glucose makes the drink taste sweet so the child will drink more
options.D: Glucose feeds the good bacteria so they can repair the damaged bowel

explanation: It's like a team effort! Sodium and glucose hitch a ride together on the same transport protein. As glucose is absorbed, it pulls sodium and water right along with it into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T57#GNS214_U1_T57_h3)

question: Which specific protein in the intestine makes Oral Rehydration Therapy work so well?

options.A: SGLT1
options.B: Gastric lipase
options.C: Potassium pump
options.D: Insulin receptor

explanation: SGLT1 (sodium-glucose linked transporter type 1) is the hero protein! It links sugar and salt uptake in the small intestine to pull precious water into the body. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T57#GNS214_U1_T57_h3)

question: What is the big advantage of modern low-osmolality ORS compared to the older, stronger formula?

options.A: It reduces stool volume and the need for IV fluids
options.B: It provides all the daily vitamins a growing child needs
options.C: It tastes much sweeter and dissolves instantly in cold water
options.D: It cures bacterial infections without needing antibiotics

explanation: By lowering the sugar and salt slightly, the modern formula creates less osmotic pull in the gut, which means less watery stool and fewer trips to the hospital for drips! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T57#GNS214_U1_T57_h4)

question: Why did health experts lower the amount of sugar in the standard ORS formula over time?

options.A: To save manufacturing costs for pharmaceutical companies
options.B: To make the powder dissolve faster in contaminated water
options.C: To stop children from developing diabetes during illness
options.D: To prevent excess sugar from pulling extra water back into the gut

explanation: Too much sugar actually acts like a sponge, drawing water back out into the stool. Lowering the sugar keeps the fluid moving safely into the body instead! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T57#GNS214_U1_T57_h4)

question: A toddler is brought to the clinic with sunken eyes, fussiness, and drinks the ORS eagerly. How would you classify this dehydration?

options.A: Chronic malnutrition
options.B: Severe dehydration
options.C: Some dehydration
options.D: No dehydration

explanation: You got it! Irritability, sunken eyes, and drinking eagerly are classic signs of moderate ('some') dehydration. Giving ORS right here in the clinic will help them bounce back. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T57#GNS214_U1_T57_h5)

question: Which of these clinical signs tells you a child has SEVERE dehydration?

options.A: Lethargy or floppiness and sluggish skin pinch
options.B: Restless behavior and dry oral mucosa
options.C: Eager and rapid drinking from a cup
options.D: Normal tear production when crying

explanation: When a child is very sleepy, floppy, or their skin pinch takes a long time to go back, that's a red flag for severe fluid loss requiring urgent medical help. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T57#GNS214_U1_T57_h5)

question: What happens if a caregiver mixes an ORS sachet in way too little water?

options.A: The child will refuse to drink because the solution is too cold
options.B: The extra salt crystals will kill all the bacteria in the stomach
options.C: The concentrated solution can worsen dehydration by drawing water into the gut
options.D: The medicine works twice as fast to stop the watery stool

explanation: Measurements matter! Too little water makes the drink too salty (hypertonic), which actually pulls body water out into the intestines and makes dehydration worse. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T57#GNS214_U1_T57_h6)
