options.A: Manufacturing sterile surgical instruments in the clinic kitchen
options.B: Isolating entire towns when a single flu case is reported
options.C: Educating families on hygiene, sanitation, and vaccination
options.D: Prescribing high-dose antibiotics without consulting a doctor

explanation: Community nurses empower everyday people with the practical knowledge needed to stop infections at home. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T95#GNS214_U1_T95_h8)

question: A nurse working in a rural primary health clinic notices an increase in skin infections among children. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Close the clinic permanently until a modern hospital is built nearby
options.B: Investigate local hygiene practices and provide health education on hand washing
options.C: Order expensive laboratory tests from overseas for every sick child
options.D: Tell parents that skin infections cannot be prevented in rural areas

explanation: The nurse begins by assessing the community's hygiene habits and teaching simple, effective prevention strategies to stop the outbreak. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T95#GNS214_U1_T95_h8)

question: What makes droplet nuclei so tricky when it comes to spreading infections?

options.A: Blocking the entry of viruses into the upper respiratory tract
options.B: Causing localized skin infections through direct contact
options.C: Settling immediately on nearby surfaces within one meter
options.D: Carrying airborne infectious pathogens over long distances

explanation: Great job thinking about how germs travel! Droplet nuclei are tiny dried-out particles that stay floating in the air for a long time, letting them travel far on air currents. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h1)

question: Why can't nurses rely on regular surgical masks when caring for patients with airborne diseases?

options.A: Surgical masks trap moisture and destroy bacterial filters
options.B: Pathogens are small enough to pass through regular mask material
options.C: Droplet nuclei can easily bypass loose-fitting surgical masks
options.D: Surgical masks only protect against blood splashes

explanation: You've got this! Regular surgical masks aren't tightly sealed enough around the edges, meaning those sneaky floating droplet nuclei can slip right past them. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h1)

question: Which of these bacterial airborne illnesses is still a major health concern across Nigeria?

options.A: Cholera
options.B: Malaria
options.C: Tuberculosis
options.D: Tetanus

explanation: Spot on! Tuberculosis (TB) is a bacterial infection that affects the lungs and remains a huge focus for public health and nursing here in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h2)

question: If a Nigerian community suddenly sees an outbreak of measles, what is the most likely cause?

options.A: Low routine immunization coverage among children
options.B: High mosquito vector breeding during the rainy season
options.C: Unsafe disposal of hospital sharp instruments
options.D: Contaminated local drinking water supplies

explanation: Well done! Measles is totally preventable with vaccines, so sudden outbreaks usually mean kids in the area are missing their routine shots. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h2)

question: What is a classic warning sign that a patient might have pulmonary tuberculosis?

options.A: Painful ulcers forming inside the oral cavity
options.B: Yellow discoloration of the sclera and skin
options.C: Sudden swelling of the lower extremities
options.D: A persistent cough lasting more than two weeks

explanation: That's right! Whenever a patient walks in with a cough that just won't quit for over two weeks, TB should immediately pop into your nursing mind. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h3)

question: A patient arrives at your clinic with a long-term cough, heavy night sweats, and sudden weight loss. What should you do first?

options.A: Placing the patient in isolation precautions
options.B: Scheduling an immediate abdominal ultrasound
options.C: Checking the patient for peripheral edema
options.D: Administering intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation: Safety first! Those classic signs point right to TB, so your immediate priority is protecting everyone else in the clinic by isolating the patient. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h3)

question: Why do nurses collect a sputum sample from a patient they suspect has tuberculosis?

options.A: To test for acid-fast bacilli and confirm infection
options.B: To check for elevated white blood cell counts
options.C: To determine the patient's blood electrolyte levels
options.D: To measure the exact oxygen saturation in the lungs

explanation: You're doing great! Sputum microscopy looks specifically for acid-fast bacilli, which are the telltale bacteria responsible for causing TB. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h4)

question: Why is it so important to tell a patient to cough up deep lung mucus instead of just spitting out mouth saliva for a TB test?

options.A: Deep-lung samples prevent the patient from coughing blood
options.B: Saliva damages the expensive laboratory testing equipment
options.C: Saliva does not contain the actual bacteria from the lungs
options.D: Saliva samples take much longer to process in the lab

explanation: Makes total sense, right? TB lives deep in the lungs, so mouth saliva won't show us the bacteria we need to find for an accurate diagnosis. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h4)

question: What special type of room ventilation is a must-have for patients on airborne precautions?

options.A: Positive pressure room
options.B: Standard natural ventilation room
options.C: Negative pressure room
options.D: Reverse isolation airflow room

explanation: Spot on! Negative pressure rooms act like a trap—when the door opens, air rushes in instead of letting infectious germs float out into the hospital hallway. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h5)

question: A patient with active TB needs to go for an X-ray in another part of the hospital. What must the nurse do?

options.A: Ensure the patient wears an N95 respirator mask
options.B: Have the patient wear a standard surgical mask
options.C: Transport the patient during peak visiting hours
options.D: Instruct the patient to hold their breath in hallways

explanation: You've got this! Putting a simple surgical mask on the patient catches their respiratory droplets right at the source while they are moving through the hospital. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h5)

question: In a busy clinic with limited resources, what is one of the best ways to reduce airborne germ spread?

options.A: Turning off ceiling fans to stop particle circulation
options.B: Installing expensive high-efficiency particulate air scrubbers
options.C: Sealing all clinical rooms to prevent outside air entry
options.D: Ensuring optimal natural ventilation by opening windows and doors

explanation: Simple and effective! When high-tech ventilation isn't available, opening up doors and windows lets fresh outdoor air sweep those germs away. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h6)

question: Why does quickly sorting (triage) a coughing patient help stop airborne infections in a crowded clinic?

options.A: It isolates infectious individuals away from the general waiting crowd
options.B: It eliminates the need for any staff personal protective equipment
options.C: It immediately cures the underlying respiratory infection
options.D: It guarantees that laboratory test results return within minutes

explanation: Brilliant nursing logic! Spotting coughing patients early and moving them away from other waiting patients stops germs from spreading in the waiting room. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h6)

question: What is the correct way to practice good cough etiquette to stop airborne germs from spreading?

options.A: Covering the face tightly with bare hands during a cough
options.B: Turning the head downward toward shared floor surfaces
options.C: Sputum expulsion directly into open waste bins
options.D: Covering the mouth and nose with a tissue or the inner elbow

explanation: Exactly! Using a tissue or coughing into your inner elbow keeps those germs off your hands so you don't pass them to door handles or other people. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h7)

question: Why is fighting social stigma just as important as giving medicine when dealing with airborne diseases?

options.A: Social isolation changes the physical structure of droplet nuclei
options.B: Community rumors replace the need for diagnostic laboratory tests
options.C: Fear of discrimination often causes patients to delay seeking care
options.D: Stigma directly inactivates the bacteria inside the lungs

explanation: So true! When people are afraid of being judged or stigmatized, they hide their sickness and stay away from clinics, which unfortunately lets the disease spread further. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T96#GNS214_U1_T96_h7)

question: What do we call a non-living object—like a stethoscope, door handle, or bed sheet—that can pass germs from one person to another?

options.A: Reservoir
options.B: Vector
options.C: Carrier
options.D: Fomite

explanation: You've got this! Non-living items that carry germs around are called fomites. Think of things like dirty linens or blood pressure cuffs moving microbes from patient to patient. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h1)

question: Which of these is a classic example of indirect contact transmission?

options.A: A nurse catches scabies after handling a patient without gloves
options.B: A farmer develops a hookworm infection walking barefoot in soil
options.C: A baby gets pinkeye (conjunctivitis) from touching a contaminated toy
options.D: A student inhales droplet nuclei from a classmate coughing

explanation: Spot on! Indirect contact happens when you pick up germs from an object (like a toy) rather than touching an infected person directly. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h1)

question: Which of these common infections spreads mainly through direct skin-to-skin touch?

options.A: Scabies
options.B: Cholera
options.C: Tuberculosis
options.D: Tetanus

explanation: Scabies is caused by tiny mites that love to crawl from one person's skin straight onto another during close contact. Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h2)

question: Why do hospital cleaners and nurses wipe down bed rails and bedside tables so often?

options.A: Air currents deposit airborne droplets directly onto these objects
options.B: Patients spend most of their recovery time touching these areas
options.C: Microorganisms multiply rapidly on metal surfaces without moisture
options.D: These surfaces act as common fomites for indirect contact spread

explanation: Exactly! High-touch areas easily collect germs from hands and pass them along to the next person, which is why cleaning them stops indirect spread. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h2)

question: What are the main germs responsible for common skin infections like boils and impetigo?

options.A: Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacilli
options.B: Staphylococcus and Streptococcus bacteria
options.C: Enteric viruses and parasites
options.D: Dermatophyte fungi and molds

explanation: Staph and Strep are the usual suspects behind those painful, pus-filled skin sores you see so often in clinic rotations. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h3)

question: A primary school pupil comes in with round, scaly, itchy patches on their head and some hair loss in those spots. What's the most likely issue?

options.A: Tinea capitis
options.B: Herpes labialis
options.C: Scabies infestation
options.D: Cellulitis

explanation: You guessed it! Circular, scaly spots with broken hair on the scalp are the trademark signs of Tinea capitis (scalp ringworm). [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h3)

question: Why does the itching from a scabies infestation usually feel way worse at night?

options.A: The body has a delayed immune reaction to mite activity
options.B: Fomites release more spores in the dark
options.C: Dry night air increases surface skin cracking
options.D: Lower nighttime temperatures activate bacterial toxins

explanation: That torturous night itch is actually your body's allergic immune response fighting off the proteins and waste left behind by the busy little mites. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h4)

question: How does a fungal skin infection get that classic ring shape?

options.A: Blood vessels constrict in a circular pattern around the pathogen
options.B: The body pushes all bacteria outward toward the skin edge
options.C: Tight clothing creates circular friction marks on the epidermis
options.D: The fungus grows outward from a center point while healing in the middle

explanation: Think of it like ripples in a pond: the fungus spreads outward in a circle to feed, leaving a clearer, healing center behind. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h4)

question: What quick bedside test helps confirm if a skin rash is caused by a fungus?

options.A: Gram stain of blood cultures
options.B: Complete blood cell count
options.C: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
options.D: Potassium hydroxide (KOH) wet mount

explanation: Spot on! Adding KOH melts away the skin cells while leaving the stubborn fungal threads clearly visible under a microscope. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h5)

question: Why is asking about family and home life so important when assessing a patient with a skin rash?

options.A: It replaces the need for a physical skin examination
options.B: It helps identify if other household members share the same contact infection
options.C: It determines the exact antibiotic resistance profile of the organism
options.D: It proves whether the patient has a genetic predisposition to eczema

explanation: Contact infections love to bounce around families! Checking if others at home are scratching stops the vicious cycle of reinfection. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h5)

question: What is the standard prescription cream applied from the neck down to treat scabies?

options.A: Hydrocortisone 1% ointment
options.B: Permethrin 5% cream
options.C: Clotrimazole antifungal lotion
options.D: Zinc oxide barrier paste

explanation: Permethrin 5% is our go-to weapon. Applied properly from the neck down, it safely wipes out both the mites and their eggs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h6)

question: A patient is treated for scabies in your clinic. What must you tell them about the rest of people living in their house?

options.A: Family members should take oral antibiotics to prevent secondary boils
options.B: Household members only need treatment if they sleep in the same bed
options.C: Only family members who are scratching should visit the clinic for cream
options.D: All household contacts must be treated at the same time, regardless of symptoms

explanation: You've got it! Because scabies spreads before itching starts, treating everyone under the roof at the same time is the only way to kick it out for good. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h6)

question: What is the single most important action to stop contact infections from spreading in a hospital?

options.A: Administering prophylactic antibiotics to all new admissions
options.B: Wearing sterile surgical masks during visiting hours
options.C: Proper hand hygiene before and after patient contact
options.D: Changing bed linens twice daily for every patient

explanation: Never underestimate simple handwashing! It is your absolute best defense against carrying germs between patients. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h7)

question: When should a nurse put on a disposable gown and gloves for contact precautions?

options.A: Immediately before leaving the isolation ward
options.B: Before entering the patient's room or care area
options.C: Only when performing open wound dressing changes
options.D: After touching contaminated hospital bed rails

explanation: Always gown and glove up *before* stepping into the room. That way, your clothes and hands stay clean right from the start. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h7)

question: Why is teaching children not to share personal items so important in schools?

options.A: Teachers are legally required to diagnose skin conditions during morning assembly
options.B: Children frequently exchange items like combs and caps, spreading fungal and parasitic infections
options.C: Sharing clothes is the only known method of bacterial transmission
options.D: Schools lack the budget to buy chemical disinfectants for classroom desks

explanation: Kids love sharing caps and combs, which unfortunately makes it super easy to pass around things like lice and ringworm! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h8)

question: Which community action has the best long-term impact on controlling contact infections?

options.A: Promoting personal hygiene and discouraging the sharing of towels and clothing
options.B: Providing free multivitamins to every household once a year
options.C: Sprinkling strong chemical insecticides on all open community grounds
options.D: Isolating all infected community members in distant rural camps

explanation: Education is key! Teaching communities good hygiene habits stops outbreaks right at the roots so they don't keep coming back. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T97#GNS214_U1_T97_h8)
